  Distance and Velocity                              A ball is thrown vertically upward from the ledge of a building 192 feet high with an ini-
                                                     tial velocity of 96 feet per second. How high will the ball go? Assume that the height of
                                                     the ball as a function of time is s1t2 = -16t2 + 96t + 192.
                                                     Solution Since we have s as a function of t already, we begin at step 5. The derivative
                                                     is s¿1t2 = -32t + 96. Setting this to zero, we find that the critical point is at t = 3.
                                                      6. s 132 6 0, thus the critical point is a relative maximum, and by the Only
                                                          Critical Point Test, a maximum. The maximum height of the ball is
                                                          s132 = -161322 + 96132 + 192 = 336 feet above the ground.


                                                     In Section 2.7 we solved similar problems by setting the velocity v = 0. From a physical
                                                     point of view, the ball will reach its maximum height at the instant when its velocity is
                                                     zero. Thus, the physical and mathematical explanations are in complete agreement.

     Price, Demand                                   ative that are usually considered theorems in micro-economics. Our first example shall
      and Revenue                                    deal with the revenue available to a monopolist. That is, we consider a market situation in
                                                     which there is no competition. Hence, the quantity and sales price of a commodity is not
                                                     the market equilibrium point determined by supply and demand curves. Instead, we have
                                                     only a demand curve, and the price is set by the monopolist producer.

To complete the problem, we must find the price per car when the revenue is maximized.
When x = 10,000, the price per car, p = -10110,0002 + 200,000 = $100,000. That is,
the optimum strategy for the manufacturer is to produce 10,000 cars to sell at $100,000

  Elasticity of Demand                                       Given a demand function, suppose we solve for x in terms of p and write this rela-
                                                     tionship as x = D1p2. The derivative, dx/dp measures the change in demand with respect
                                                     to price. However, this is not a very useful measure as it is dependent upon the units used.
                                                     For example, suppose x is measured in tons and p in dollars and dx/dp = 2 tons per dol-
                                                     lar. If we change our units of measurement from tons to pounds, then the value of dx/dp is
                                                     multiplied by a factor of 2000 making it 4000 pounds per dollar. Certainly, if we want to
                                                     measure the rate of change of demand with respect to price, our measurement should be
                                                     independent of units. To that end, we divide dx/dp by the quantity x/p, which has the same
                                                     units. The resulting ratio is a dimensionless quantity. This ratio is called the elasticity of
                                                     demand and we designate it PD.
                                                     DEFINITION 1 The elasticity of demand, denoted by PD is defined by

                                                                                                     dp  p dx

                                                                                                      p

      Note that in economic theory, demand decreases as the price increases. That is,
every demand function is a decreasing function. Therefore, dx/dp 6 0. Since both x
and p are positive it follows that the elasticity of demand will always be negative. The de-
mand is called elastic if PD 7 1, and the demand is inelastic if PD 6 1. If PD = 1,
the elasticity is said to be unitary. The reason for choosing PD = 1 as the transition
from elastic to inelastic demand will be given shortly. We first need an additional
definition.

DEFINITION 2 The relative change of a function whose equation is p = f1q2 as q
changes from q1 to q2 is

                                                         f1q22 - f1q12
                                  relative change =                                                        (2)
                                                             f(q1)
       The percentage change is defined as
                                                   f1q22 - f1q12
                            percent change =                     * 100%                                    (3)
                                                       f(q1)
       To better understand this terminology, consider the demand equation
x = 100 - 3p. When p = 1, x = 97, when p = 2, x = 94. Thus, a one unit change in
p, from p = 1 to p = 2, represents 100% change in price. The 3 unit change in x, from
x = 97 to x = 94, represents a 3/97 or roughly a 3% change in demand. Thus a 100%
change in price causes only a 3% change in demand. The demand is relatively inflexible;
that is, it is inelastic. On the other hand, as p changes from p = 30 to p = 31, about a
3% change in price, the corresponding change in demand is from x = 10 to x = 7, a
30% change. At this price range, a small change in price results in a relatively large
change in demand. Therefore, in this price range, the demand is elastic.
       Of course, we have been analyzing the case in which the demand equation is linear.
In this case it is easy to show that the elasticity is exactly equal to the ratio of the relative
change in demand to the relative change in price (see Exercise 22). For nonlinear demand
equations the elasticity is not exactly equal to the ratio of the relative change in demand to
relative change in price, but it does give approximately this value. In fact, we may obtain
equation (1) by taking the limit of the ratio as the change in price approaches zero (see
Exercise 23). Thus, the terminology elastic and inelastic carry over naturally to nonlinear
demand functions.

                                                     mation to the function near the point of tangency. In this section, we expand upon this no-

       Let us not lose sight of the fact that linearization is nothing more than finding the
equation of the tangent line. We may now exploit this fact and use linearization as an ef-
fective tool for approximation. Our next example illustrates how this may be done, but we
must point out it is much easier and probably more accurately done by a calculator. How-
ever, the purpose of the example is to illustrate the method of linearization. Linearization
is used to replace a complicated expression by a simpler one. The next example illustrates
that once this is done, calculations are especially simple.

      Thus, P measures the difference between the slope of the (secant) line through P
and Q and the slope of the tangent line at P. For a differentiable function, this difference
                                                                                                                                     Differentiable Functions
approaches zero as ¢x = h approaches zero. In fact we may define differentiability of a
function as follows.

DEFINITION 3 A function whose equation is y = f1x2 is differentiable if the change
in y may be written in the form

                                          ¢y = D ¢x + P ¢x                                                 (6)
where P approaches zero as ¢x approaches zero. D is then the derivative of the function.
       It is precisely this observation that is used to generalize the definition of differentia-
bility to a function of several variables. Exercise 33 illustrates how (6) may be used to
prove the chain rule.
       We now see that the differential gives the approximate change in y for a small
change in x. However, there is a little more to it than that. Consider, once again, the case

       Using this new terminology, it is now possible to rewrite all our derivative formulas
as differential formulas. All the rules for derivatives will carry through to differentials.
Thus, for instance, the differential of a sum is the sum of the differentials because the de-
rivative of a sum is the sum of the derivatives. Or, for example, if we have y = xN, then

                                                     Recall that in the definition of a function defined by the equation y = f1x2 we required
                                                     that to each x-value there correspond a unique y-value. Suppose the function is
                                                     f = 51 - 1, 32, 10, 72, 12, 42, 15, 326, what about the set we obtain by interchanging the
                                                     x and y values? Is it also a function? The set obtained is 513, -12, 17, 02, 14, 22, 13, 526.
                                                     Observe both 13, - 12 and (3, 5) belong to this set, therefore it cannot be a function (Why?).
                                                     What can we do to insure that the set obtained by interchanging the coordinates also yields
                                                     a function? It should be clear that we need the second set to satisfy the uniqueness property
                                                     as well. This translates into a very simple statement regarding the original function.
                                                           A function defined by the equation y = f1x2 is said to be a one-to-one function if
                                                     (in addition to each x corresponding to a unique y) each y-value corresponds to a unique
  One-to-One Function                                x-value. We may rephrase this by saying that the only way two y-values are the same is if
                                                     their x-values are the same; we may write this condition as follows: if f1x12 = f1x22
                                                     then we must have x1 = x2. (Or equivalently as: if x1 Z x2 then f1x12 Z f1x22.)

                                                     Example 1
                                                     Is the linear function defined by the equation f1x2 = 3x + 7 one-to-one?
                                                     Solution
                                                     Suppose we have f1x12 = f1x22, that is 3x1 + 7 = 3x2 + 7, then it follows from this
                                                     equation that
                                                                                                     3x1 = 3x2
                                                     or
                                                                                                       x 1 = x2
                                                     thus, the function is one-to one, since the only way two y-values are the same is if their
                                                     x-values are.


                                                           The notion of a function being one-to-one is easily determined from its graph. Since
                                                     the condition states that different x-values correspond to different y-values, it means for a
  Horizontal Line Test                               function to be one-to-one, no horizontal line drawn through the graph can intersect it in
                                                     more than one point. If it did, then the same y-value would correspond to two different
                                                     x-values, contrary to the definition of a function being one-to-one. This observation is
                                                     called the horizontal line test.

                                                     Example 2
                                                     From the sketch of the graph of f1x2 = 3x + 7, show the function is one-to-one.
                                                     Solution The sketch of the graph is given in Figure 1.

Example 3
Determine if the function whose equation is given by y = f1x2 = 2x2 + 1 is one-to-one.
Solution The graph of the function is the parabola indicated in Figure 2. Note that any
horizontal line that is not drawn through the vertex of the parabola, intersects the graph in
two points or not at all. Therefore, by the horizontal line test, this is not the graph of a
one-to-one function.


It should be noted in the previous example, that we could just as well have applied the
definition of a function being one-to-one to show that the given function is not one-to-one.

the horizontal line test we see that a horizontal line will intersect a graph in more than one
point if the graph has a turning point. This is illustrated in Figure 2. Therefore, as long as                                            Increasing and
a graph does not turn (that is, the graph has no relative extrema), a horizontal line will only                                        Decreasing Functions

                                                           Let us return to question posed earlier. Under what conditions can we interchange
                                                     the x and y-values and have the new set thus obtained also be a function? From the above
                                                     discussions we see that the original function must be a one-to-one function.

                                                     Example 4
                                                     Is the set obtained by interchanging the x and y-values in each of the given functions also
                                                     a function? (a) f = 51- 3, 22, 10, 52, 11, -72, 13, 22, 15, 1126, (b) g = 51-1, 42,
                                                     12, 32, 13, 82, 15, 2026
                                                     Solution
                                                     (a) If we interchange the x and y-values, we obtain 512, -32, 15, 02, 1-7, 12, 12, 32,
                                                         111, 526. This is not a function, the set obtained violates the uniqueness property of
                                                         the definition of a function. This occurs because f is not a one-to-one function as
                                                         y = 2 corresponds to two different x-values, namely - 3 and 3.
                                                     (b) The function g is a one-to-one function since each y-value corresponds to exactly one
                                                         x-value. Therefore the set obtained by interchanging x with y, 514, -12, 13, 22,
                                                         18, 32, 120, 526 is also a function.


                                                     Observe that the first derivative test can be very useful in classifying increasing and decreas-
                                                     ing function. Recall that on any interval on which the derivative is positive, the function is
                                                     increasing and on any interval on which the derivative is negative, the function is decreasing.

                                                     Example 5
                                                     Show that the function defined by the equation y = f1x2 = 4x3 + 9x - 7 is a one-to-
                                                     one function.
                                                     Solution We have f¿1x2 = 12x2 + 9 7 0 for all x. (Why?) Therefore, f is an increas-
                                                     ing function over its entire domain and, therefore, a one-to-one function.

The function obtained by interchanging the x-values with the y-values is called the inverse
function. More formally we have the following: Given the one-to-one function defined by
                                                                                                                                          Inverse Function
the equation y = f1x2, the function obtained by interchanging every x and every y-value is
called the inverse function. We write the equation of the inverse function as y = f -11x2*.
(Note that the function must be one-to-one in order for the inverse function to be defined.)

      Observe that the function and its inverse are mirror images about the line y = x.
This is true in general. Namely, given any one-to-one function, the reflection of this func-
tion about the line y = x yields the graph of its inverse function.
      We now consider the determination of the equation of the inverse function. We ob-
served that the inverse function is determined by interchanging every x and y coordinate.
That means we need only interchange x and y in the equation of the original function to
obtain the equation of the inverse function.

     Summary
     Given the one-to-one function y * f1x2
      1. The inverse function, y * f +11x2 exists.
      2. The graph of the inverse function is obtained from the graph of the original
         function by interchanging its x and y-coordinates. (The graph of y * f +11x2
         will be the mirror image of the graph of y * f1x2 using the line y * x as
         the mirror.)
      3. The domain of f becomes the range of f +1.
      4. The range of f becomes the domain of f +1.
      5. The equation of the inverse is determined by (a) interchanging y with x in the
         equation y * f1x2, and (b) solving the equation x * f1y2 for y.


      We remark that sometimes, it is necessary to define new functions to implement
Step 5, as we shall see later on in this chapter.
      Inverse functions satisfy a unique property with regard to their composition with
each other. Consider Figure 7 where we have the graph of y = f1x2 and its inverse
                                                                                                                                       Composition Property

on the graph of y = f -11x2.

Consider the exponential expression 2x. When x is a rational number 2x is well-defined.
For example, expressions like 22/3, or 2-3/2 make perfectly good sense. What do we mean
by the expression when x is irrational? We do not intend to give a rigorous definition here,
but rather be guided by our intuition. For example, how could we define 222? To ten deci-
mal places, we have 22 L 1.4142135624, and we have that
     21.4 =                  2.639015822
     21.41 =                 2.657371628
     21.414 =                2.664749650
     21.4142 =               2.665119099
     21.41421 =              2.665137562
     21.414213 =             2.665143104
     21.4142135 =            2.665144027
     21.41421356 =           2.665144138
     21.414213562 =          2.665144142
     21.4142135624 =         2.665144143
and so on. It is clear, that as we take more and more places, the value of 222 is, to seven
decimal places, 2.6651441. We could analyze any irrational power the same way. Fortu-                                                Exponential Expressions
nately, these powers can be computed with our calculator. Thus, using a calculator, we
would obtain 222 = 2.665144. We now assume that any number of the form bx, where b
is any positive number other than 1 and x is any real number, is well defined. As a conse-
quence, all the laws of exponents given for rational exponents will be satisfied for irra-
tional exponents as well.
       Note: we exclude b from being 1, since 1 raised to any finite power is 1, certainly a
trivial example. b is not allowed to be negative because we want to deal only with real
numbers for example, 1-421/2 = 2i.
       Now that we understand what we mean by expressions of the form bx, we see that
to each x-value there corresponds one y-value thus, the equation y = f1x2 = 2x defines a
function. We shall select convenient values in its domain and draw its graph. These values
are illustrated in Table 1.
       You will note that we selected convenient rational values for x, plotted and then con-
nected the points to sketch the graph. As irrational values for x lie between rational values
that we plotted, they are, by continuity, represented on the graph as well.

We now look at a different, but related problem. Consider the problem of finding x if we
are given that
                                              32x - 3 = 34 + 5x
       Since the exponential function is a one-to-one function, we have that if br = bs,
then it must follow that r = s. Thus, we observe that if the bases are the same, then so are
the exponents. Therefore, in the given problem we have that                                                                              Solving Special
                                                                                                                                      Exponential Equations
                                           2x - 3 = 4 + 5x
or solving, we find that x = -7/3. What if the bases are different? For example, suppose
the problem was to solve 32x - 3 = 54 + 5x? We will need a more general procedure to solve
such exponential equations, and we will discuss this generalized problem when we define
the logarithm. However, there is one special case in which the bases are different, but
using some simple properties of exponents, the equation may be modified to an equivalent
one in which the bases are the same. We illustrate in the next two examples.

                                                                                                  29x + 12 = 232 - 12x
                                                     We have now changed the equation into an equivalent one in which the bases are the
                                                     same, therefore, we have that

                                                           Let us examine exponential functions a little more closely so we can develop a

Finding the Exponential
                                                     The first observation is that an exponential function has the property that for equally
       Function
                                                     spaced x-values, the ratio of successive y-values is constant. Consider Table 1.
                                                                      Table 1: Equally Spaced x-value with Constant Ratios in

It is important not to confuse an exponential expression which has the form bx with a
power expression, one of the form xk, where k is a constant. Note that for an exponential
expression, the base is the constant and the power is the variable, whereas for a power ex-
pression the base is the variable and the power is the constant. A power function has an                                                   Power Function
equation of the form f1x2 = ax b. Exponential and power functions grow (and decay) dif-
ferently. In Section 2.4 we shall examine this remark more fully, but for now, we state that
exponential functions dominate power functions, that is, they grow more quickly and
decay more rapidly. We shall illustrate this comparison in the Example 7 below where we
model a data set three ways.
       The calculator makes computations with exponential expression very straight-for-
ward. To compute the value of an exponential expression we enter it normally and use the
caret key ¿ to denote exponentiation, thus, to compute 126-2.3 we enter 126¿1-2.32 and                                                     Calculator Tips
press enter.

So which one model do we choose, the linear, exponential or power curve? If we had ad-
ditional data, then the answer would be the one that best supports the data. For example,
suppose x in the above data set represented years and f(x) represented the population in
year x. Let us also suppose that we know that in year x = 10, the population was 5. Using
the linear model we obtain 3.971, the exponential yields 4.49 and the power model yields
3.277. It appears that the exponential better models the data than either the line or the
power.
       Also note that as x gets large, the exponential values grow much faster than either
the linear or power values. For example, compare values for x = 100, 1000 and so on.
This demonstrates that exponential growth dominates linear and power growth.

      The constant e did not appear in the early study of finance. The first reference to the
constant was in 1618 in the work of John Napier. It was the mathematician Euler who first
represented the constant by the letter e in 1727.
      The base of any positive exponent can be written in terms of e, that is, we can find a
number k such that
                                                   b = ek
       For example, if the base is 2, then 2 = ek, and k is approximately 0.693147. The de-
termination of k requires the taking of a logarithm, to be considered later on in this chap-
ter. Thus, any base can be replaced by base e with an appropriate k. Base e is so important
to calculus that it is called the natural base. Using it, we shall see, simplifies calculations
in the calculus.
       As mentioned above, to access the ex key on the calculator, we press * and then X.
We can use the TI 89 to graph any exponential function. For example, we can enter in the
                                                                                                                                            Calculator Tips
Y = screen, y11x2 = e ¿1-2x2. Making sure the calculator has an appropriate window, it
will then graph this equation.
       The remark made above was that any base b can be written in the form ek. Later on
in this chapter, we shall give an explicit formula which determines k. However, we can use
the solve command to determine k. For example, solve 12 = e ¿1k2, k2 yields (press *
Enter for a numerical answer) 0.693147.

and b are positive numbers then

      This theorem states that while the x grows very large as x : q , it is overwhelmed
by the way the exponential term approaches zero as x : q , so much so that their product
is zero. To convince yourself of this fact, examine the product x 100e -0.02x for large values                                               Exponential
of x. (Make sure you choose very large values of x, greater than 55,000 to see that the                                                      Domination
product is small. For example, when x = 55,000, the product is 0.0002053. For smaller
values of x the product is large).
      Exponential functions with negative exponents decay very quickly, much more
quickly than algebraic functions, which is why the product indicated in the theorem ap-
proaches zero. Similarly, exponential functions with positive exponents grow very
quickly. That is why the companion statement to the theorem is
                                             lim x -aebx = q                                               (6)
                                            x: q
       Basically, these two results indicate that an exponential function rises and decays
much more quickly than most functions. In particular, an exponential will grow much
faster and decay more quickly than a polynomial function.

      Since this is an increasing function it is one-to-one, and, therefore, it has an inverse.
Before we discuss the equation of the inverse let us make some observations about the
function and its inverse.
    y * f1x2 * 2x                                          y * f +11x2
   Domain: - q 6 x 6 q                                     Domain: x 7 0
   Range: y 7 0                                            Range: q 6 y 6 q
   Graph passes through (0, 1)                             Graph passes through (1, 0)
       We may draw the graph of the inverse function by interchanging the points used to
plot the original function. This graph obtained by the interchange is given in Figure 2.




                            Figure 2: The Inverse of y = f1x2 = 2x

     The analysis for an arbitrary exponential function and its inverse is almost identical.
Given the function whose equation is y = f1x2 = bx where b Z 1 is a positive number
we have:
    y * f1x2 * b x                                         y * f +11x2
   Domain: - q 6 x 6 q                                     Domain: x 7 0
   Range: y 7 0                                            Range: - q 6 y 6 q
   Graph passes through (0, 1)                             Graph passes through (1, 0)
       The graph for the inverse function may be obtained from the graph of the exponen-
tial function by interchanging the x and the y coordinates.
       The unanswered question at this point is the determination of the equation of the in-
verse function in the form y = f -11x2. Before we give the equation we make an observa-
tion about defining functions. Sometimes, it is convenient to define new functions. You
might seem surprised by this statement, but it is something with which you are familiar.
Suppose we ask you to write the positive number whose square is 5. Without thinking,
you would write 25. However, this is only a representative symbol, in fact we could just
as well have written the symbol as SQRT (5). The statement x = 25 is equivalent to the
statement x2 = 5 (and x 7 0). Similarly, the statement y = 1x is equivalent to the
statement that y is the positive solution to the equation y 2 = x. The square root symbol
was introduced so that we could solve this last equation for y in terms of x. That is, the
symbol y = 1x is equivalent to x = y2 (and y 7 0).
       We can now go back to our question. Given the equation y = f1x2 = 2x, how do
we determine the equation of its inverse function? We proceed exactly as we have learned
before: we first interchange x with y and write x = f1y2 = 2y. The problem that now
arises is how do we solve this equation for y in terms of x. We do this by defining a new
function! The solution to the equation x = 2y is y = log 2 x. Thus we have that the fol-
lowing two equivalent expressions; namely

For special types of problems switching from the logarithmic to the exponential form of
the expression is useful, as we illustrate in the next example.

Example 3
Compute log 3 27.
Solution Let log 3 27 = x, rewriting this expression in exponential format, we have
3x = 27. This is a special exponential equation which is easily solved by writing 3x = 33,
or x = 3.


It should be noted that if the base of the logarithm was different from 3 then the resulting
exponential function could not be easily solved. We shall examine such cases shortly.
       There are two special bases deserving special attention, namely base 10 and base e.
Logarithms to the base 10 are called common logarithms and those to base e are called nat-
                                                                                                                                            Base 10 and e
ural logarithms. Often, when base 10 is used, we write log instead of log 10 and when base
e is used, we write ln instead of log e. Thus log x means log 10 x and ln x means log e x.

Four basic properties of logarithms

                                                      format as bx = b = b1, therefore x = 1. Properties (3) and (4) follow immediately from

                                                             Calculators provide log and ln keys, so by using them we can quickly compute loga-
                                                      rithms to these bases. The TI-89 has the ln key above the X in orange and the log key is in
                                                      the catalog. For example, using the calculator, we have, to seven decimal places,
                                                      ln 14 = 2.6390573 and log 23 = 1.3617278.
                                                             Thus, using a calculator, it is a simple matter to compute logarithms or to plot the
                                                      graphs of logarithms to base 10 or e. (Other bases will be examined in the next section.)
                                                             Logarithms arise in a variety of applications. Consider the following example from
                                                      chemistry. The acidity of a solution was originally viewed as the concentration of the hy-
    pH of a Solution                                  dronium ion H 3O + present in it, indicated by [H 3O +]. Since the concentration can change
                                                      over several orders of magnitude, it is convenient to use a logarithmic scale. This idea was
                                                      used by the Swedish chemist S. P. L. Sorenson when in 1909 he defined the pH of a solu-
                                                      tion, expressed in logarithmic notation, as
                                                                                                 pH = - log[H 3O +]                                              (3)
                                                                     +
                                                      where [H 3O ] represents the concentration of the ion. The pH is usually given to the near-
                                                      est tenth.
                                                             If the pH of a solution is less than 7, the solution is called acidic; if the pH is
                                                      about 7, the solution is neutral; if the pH is greater than 7, the solution is is called basic.

                                                      Example 4
                                                      Determine the pH of a solution whose hydronium ion concentration is 4.2 * 10-11.
                                                      Solution Substituting into (3), we have

                                                                                             pH = - log 4.2 * 10-11.
                                                      Using a calculator we obtain (to the nearest tenth) pH = 10.4. This solution is basic since
                                                      the pH exceeds 7.

       If a data set appears to resemble a logarithmic curve, or if for some other reason, we
suspect that the data is logarithmic, then we may determine a best fit regression equa-
tion just as we did for linear, power and exponential functions. Suppose we are given the
following data set:
                          (1, 0.13), (2, 0.65), (3, 1.16), (4, 1.29), (5, 1.71)
     We fit this data to a logarithmic regression curve done exactly the same way on the
TI 89 as you would for linear (or quadratic) with the only change being we replace
LinReg with LnReg. We proceed as follows:
(1) Store the x-coordinates and y-coordinates as lists named t1 and t2, as follows:                                 Figure 9: Defining Log on the TI 89
    51, 2, 3, 4, 56 STO t1 press ENTER
    50.13, 0.65, 1.15, 1.29, 1.716 STO t2 press ENTER
    Make sure you are using curly braces to enclose these two lists
(2) Next enter on the entry line of the HOME screen (use the Catalog or type)
    LnReg t1, t2 and press ENTER
    then
    ShowStat and press ENTER (This produces Figure 10)
(3) To draw the regression curve, enter on the entry line in the HOME screen,

Historically, when logarithms were first defined, one of their most important uses was to
calculate products, quotients and powers of large numbers. They were able to be used for
this purpose because of their basic properties which we shall discuss. With the appearance
of the calculator, many of the calculations using logarithms are now no longer needed, but
                                                   1620313221000
not all of them. For example try to calculate ln                  ; most calculators will indi-
                                                    2.5.000000003
cate that this number is outside of its range. However, with the application of some simple
properties, this logarithm may be easily computed, as we shall see. Moreover, these prop-
erties are invaluable in the study of the calculus of the logarithm.
       Let A and B be positive numbers, then
                                     log b AB = log b A + log b B                                          (1)
                                              A                                                                                          Multiplicative and
                                      log b     = log b A - log b B                                        (2)
                                              B                                                                                          Division Properties
      In college algebra, proof of these properties is usually given by rewriting the loga-
rithmic expression in exponential format (see Exercises 103 104), here, we take a differ-
ent approach.
      First, we recall that when we studied the first derivative test, we observed that if the
derivative is zero (on some interval) then the function is a constant (on that interval). We
can use this observation to show that if two functions have the same derivative, they differ
at most by a constant. Suppose in particular that
                                               f¿1x2 = g¿1x2
Let
                                         D1x2 = f1x2 - g1x2
then
                                    D¿1x2 = f¿1x2 - g¿1x2 = 0,
therefore, it follows that
                                                 D1x2 = c
or
                                              f1x2 - g1x2 = c


      We are now in a position to prove the various properties of logarithms. We prove the
properties for natural logarithms, that is, base e. Verification for any other base follows from
the change of base theorem that we give later on this section and will be left as an exercise.

In the next example we use the properties of logarithms to determine the time it takes an
investment to reach a specified accumulation.

Example 9
How long does it take $1000 to accumulate to $1650 if money is earning interest at a rate
of 12% per year, compounded (a) monthly; (b) continuously?
Solution Let t be the time in years.
(a) We have, using the compound interest formula, A = P11 + r/n2nt,
                      1650 = 100011 + 0.12/12212t, or 1.650 = 11.01212t.
     We solve this exponential equation by taking the logarithm of each side of the equa-
     tion Thus,
                                ln 1.65 = ln11.01212t = 12t ln 1.01.
     or
                          t = ln 1.65/112 ln 1.012 = 4.193958432 years.
    We may compute t to the nearest day as follows: The fraction, 0.193958432 years
    is equal to 0.193958432 # 12 months = 2.327501194 months. This gives 2 months
    and the remaining fraction, 0.327501194 months = 0.327501194 # 30 days =
    9.82503552 days. Thus, t = 4 years 2 months and 10 days, assuming 30 days per
    month. Banks always round up to the nearest day, even if the decimal portion is less
    than 0.5.
(b) Using A = Pert we have
                                 1650 = 1000e0.12t, or 1.65 = e0.12t
     Taking logarithms, we have,
                ln 1.65 = ln e0.12t = 0.12t ln e = 0.12t 1remember, ln e = 12
     or,
                              t = ln 1.65/0.12 = 4.173127399 years.
     To the nearest day, we find that t = 4 years 2 months and 3 days. Are you surprised
     that the difference is only seven days?

       Where C and k are constants to be determined by the specific application.
       We saw that any application modeled by equation (1) is said to exhibit exponential
growth if k 7 0, or decay if k 6 0, k is called the growth or decay constant, depending
                                                                                                                                        Exponential Growth
upon its sign.
       We noted that C had a simple but special interpretation. Substituting t = 0 into (1)
we have that f102 = Ce0. Since e0 = 1, we have f102 = C. C is called the initial value.
For example, if f(t) represents a population at time t, f(0) will be the initial population,
often written as P0. If f(t) represents the mass of some substance at time t, f(0) will be the
initial mass, often written as m0, and so on.
       Often, the rate of change of population is proportional to the population itself at any
time. If we let P(t) represent the population at time t, then we may rewrite (1) as
                                                                                                                                         Population Growth

which is simply equation (1) with P(t) replacing f(t) and P0 replacing C. Here is a specific
example.

Archeologists are able to determine the age of an artifact by measuring the amount of ra-
dioactive carbon it contains. The idea behind this method is very clever. A certain fraction
                                                                                                                                           Carbon Dating
of all the carbon in the world is Carbon 14, which is radioactive. When plants breath in
carbon dioxide, they absorb the carbon, which becomes incorporated into the plant s cells.
After the plant dies, it stops taking in new carbon. Thus, the amount of Carbon 14 remain-
ing in anything made of wood will depend upon the age of the article. Knowing that the
half-life of radioactive Carbon is approximately 5745 years, we are able to determine, as
in the previous example, that its decay constant k = 1ln 0.52/5745 L - 0.000121. The
next example illustrates the method.

                                                      A word about units. You will note that in Example 4, we measure t in years, and in Exam-
                                                      ple 3, it was measured in days. Notice that in (1), replacing C by f(0), the right hand side
                                                      is f(0) ekt. f(0) has the same units as f(t), thus ekt is a dimensionless quantity. On the other
                                                      hand, t has the units of time, therefore, k must have the units 1/time. Thus, if t is measured
                                                      in hours, k has units 1/hours; if t is measured in days, k is measured in 1/days, years, k is
                                                      measured in 1/years, and so on.

                                                      fraction or percentage of the population infected at time t. (The fraction not infected at
    Logistic Growth                                   time t is 1 - p1t2.) For example if 2/5 of the population is infected, 1 - 2/5 = 3/5 is not

                                                      In 1935 Charles Richter working with Dr. Beno Gutenberg developed a relationship be-
                                                      tween the magnitude M of an earthquake and the amount of energy E it radiates. The rela-
      Richter Scale                                   tionship is given by the (base 10) logarithmic equation
                                                                                              log E * 11.8 + 1.5M                                                (5)
                                                      where E is measured in ergs. As a result of the logarithmic basis of the scale, we shall see
                                                      that each whole number step in the magnitude scale corresponds to the release of almost
                                                      32 times more energy than the amount associated with the preceding whole number value.

                                                      Example 6
                                                      The 1906 earthquake in San Francisco measured 8.3 on the Richter scale. Determine the
                                                      energy of the earthquake.
                                                      Solution Substituting M = 8.3 in (5) we have

                                                                                       log E = 11.8 + 1.518.32 = 24.25
                                                      Rewriting this expression in exponential format, we have
                                                                                        E = 1024.25 L 1.78 * 1024 ergs.



                                                      Table 1 indicates the relationship between the magnitude of an earthquake and its effects.
                                                      Table 1: Richter Magnitude and Earthquake Effects
                                                           Richter Magnitude (M)           Earthquake Effects
                                                           Less than 3.5                   Recorded but generally not felt
                                                           3.5 5.4                         Felt, but rarely causes any damage.
                                                           Under 6.0                       Usually, minor damage to constructed buildings. Often results in
                                                                                           major damage to poorly constructed buildings over small areas.
                                                           6.1 6.9                         Destructive in areas up to about 65 miles across.
                                                           7.0 7.9                         Major earthquake. Can cause serious damage over larger areas
                                                           Over 8                          Great earthquake. Can cause serious damage in areas several hun-
                                                                                           dred miles across


                                                      Example 7
                                                      What is the Richter magnitude of an earthquake whose energy is 1.23 * 1019 ergs?
                                                      Solution Substituting into (5), we have

                                                                                        log 1.23 * 1019 = 11.8 + 1.5M
                                                      or
                                                                                             19.0899 = 11.8 + 1.5M
                                                      or to the nearest tenth,
                                                                                                       M = 4.9

                                                     ple, given F1x2 = 3x2 find a function f whose derivative f¿1x2 = 3x2. Possible choices
                                                     are f1x2 = x3, f1x2 = x3 - 7, f1x2 = x3 + 50, or in fact many others. Note that all
                                                     anitderivatives of 3x2 differ at most by a constant. This follows from the first derivative
                                                     test, as we discovered in Section 2.6, that if two functions have the same derivative, they
                                                     differ at most by an arbitrary constant. Thus, in the example just considered, the most gen-

Basically, this section did nothing more than restate the basic rules of differentiation in
terms of its inverse operation, antidifferentiation. The specific functions we considered
were the power, logarithmic and exponential functions, and the rules obtained were the
simple ones. The variable that appeared in each function was x; there were no composite
functions. It is clear that we will need to examine how to reverse the generalized rules for
differentiation of these three functions to integrate more complicated expressions. We
shall do so in Section 5.3.
       We restate the three simple rules, but instead of using the variable x, we use the vari-
able u. We shall see in applications, that often the independent variable is time, indicated
by t, so it is not a good idea to get used to notation which uses any particular letter to rep-
resent the variable.

We saw in the previous section that finding an integral of a function (antidifferentiation)
gives an infinite number of solutions, that is, for every different choice of the constant c
we obtain another antiderivative. In effect, the general solution we found gives rise to a                                                Particular Solutions
family of solutions. Often, in applications, we are given additional data that results in our
being able to find a particular solution which is both the antiderivative and satisfies this
additional information; then we have the so called particular solution. We illustrate with
examples.

We saw that if s = f1t2 represents position s, as a function of time t, then the first deriva-
tive represents the velocity v, at time t, and the second derivative represents the accelera-
tion a at time t. Thus, given the equation representing the position as a function of time,                                             Equations of Motion
we could differentiate and determine both the equations for velocity and acceleration, the
so-called equations of motion. We now reverse the question; suppose we are given the ac-
celeration of some object, moreover, suppose we know both the object s initial position
and velocity. Can we determine its position and velocity at any other time? We illustrate
the procedure by which we can do so with a few examples. The first example illustrates
vertical motion where the only force on the object is gravity. The acceleration due to grav-
ity g, is approximately -32 ft/sec 2 or in metric units, -9.8 m/sec 2. (The minus sign oc-
curs because we assume the usual position of our axes positive vertical position upward,
and the force of gravity is directed downward.)

Example 5
With what minimum velocity must an object be thrown upward from ground level if it is
to reach an altitude of 225 ft?
Solution We are given that s102 = 0 (the object begins from ground level) and we
wish to find v(0) if it is to reach 225 ft. Let v102 = v0. Let us turn around the problem and
for the moment assume we know the initial velocity, and instead find the maximum height
of the object. Of course we want this to be (at least) 225 feet. Proceeding as in the previ-
ous problem, we find

                                           v1t2 = -32t + v0
and
                                          s1t2 = -16t2 + v0t
When it reaches the maximum height, v = 0, so we have
                                             -32t + v0 = 0
or
                                                 t = v0/32
now we substitute to find the maximum height, so we have
                          smax = s1v0/322 = -161v0/3222 + v01v0/322
now if we set this equal to 225 (the height the object is to attain), we have
                                   -161v0/3222 + v01v0/322 = 225
or
                                               v02 = 14,400
or
                                             v0 = 120 ft/sec
Therefore an initial velocity of at least 120 ft/sec will guarantee the object will reach an
altitude of 225 ft.


Another way of solving this problem is to compute the impact velocity an object that is
dropped from a vertical elevation of 225 feet has with the ground. Why will this impact
velocity (ignoring its sign) solve the problem? See Exercise 32.

                                                                  »   Areas by Rectangles

                                                              Simplistically speaking, calculus answers two questions. The first, which we have already
                                                              studied in some detail, is how to determine the equation of the tangent line to a curve.
                                                              Most of differential calculus is just a detailed response to this question. The second ques-
                                                              tion that calculus answers is the following: find the area of the region bounded by the
                                                              graph of y = f1x2, the x-axis and the lines x = a and x = b. See Figure 1.

                         x=a                                       x=b

                   Figure 1: Area of Region Bounded by y = f1x2,
                   the x-axis and the Lines x = a and x = b


       What is interesting is that while these two questions seem to have no connection, we
shall discover that indeed they do. In order to answer the second question we begin with
                                                                                                                                        Areas by Rectangles
one simple idea, the rectangle. The area of a rectangle is defined to be the product of its
length and width. What we do now is to approximate the area of the region we are trying
to determine by rectangles. If we can cover or exhaust the area with enough contiguous
rectangles, then by summing the areas of these rectangles we should obtain a good ap-
proximation to the area of the given region. We shall see that by increasing the number of
rectangles covering the region the approximation will improve. Thinking like a mathe-
matician, you might then suggest we let the number of covering rectangles become infi-
nite (this will involve a limit), and we should then obtain the required area.

Example 1
Let us consider the problem of approximating the area A under the parabola defined by
f1x2 = x2 + 1, the x-axis, and between the lines x = 1 and x = 2, see Figure 2.

                                                     terval between x = 1 and x = 2 into n = 4 equal subdivisions (we chose four arbitrar-
                                                     ily), since the length of the original interval is 2 - 1 = 1 unit long and we want four
                                                     equal subintervals, each will have length ¢x = 12 - 12/4 = 1/4. Thus, the four subin-
                                                     tervals will be [1, 1.25], [1.25, 1.5], [1.5, 1.75], and [1.75, 2]. At each x-value on the
                                                     subintervals, we draw a vertical line from the x-axis to the curve. So we draw the lines
                                                     x = 1, x = 1.25, x = 1.5, x = 1.75 and x = 2, see Figure 3.

We now have four inscribed rectangles, each of width ¢x = 1/4 = 0.25. The height of

first rectangle is f112 = 12 + 1 = 2, the heights of the other three rectangles are

The area of each rectangle is then the height times 1/4. The sum of the areas of these four
rectangles is therefore
s4 = 1/4122 + 1/412.56252 + 1/413.252 + 1/414.06252 =
                                                     12 + 2.5625 + 3.25 + 4.062421/4 = 2.96875
Note that this sum under-approximates the area of the required region because each rec-
tangle does not fill up the entire region under the curve.

Notice the improvement in the approximation of the area by doubling the number of rec-
tangles. In each case by using more rectangles, the rectangles better filled (exhausted) the
area under the curve.
      It appears that in the above example, our approximations are getting better very
quickly, remember, we indicated that the exact answer is 10/3 L 3.3333. In the language
of mathematics, we say these sums converge quickly to the exact answer. We have agree-
ment to two decimal places with only n = 8 rectangles.
      This does not always happen, sometimes, n has to be very large before the approxi-
mation is any good. Let us consider another example.
      We know from elementary geometry that the area of a circle of radius 1 is p. The equa-
tion of the circle of radius 1 centered at the origin is given by the equation x2 + y 2 = 1.
Therefore, the upper half of this circle is given by the equation y = f1x2 = 21 - x2, and
the domain is -1        x     1. To make it even simpler, let us take one-half of this semi-circle,
that is the quarter circle in the first quadrant. So we consider the area of the region bounded                             Figure 10: The Quarter Circle
by the curve whose equation is y = f1x2 = 21 - x 2, with 0              x    1, see Figure 10.                              y = f1x2 = 21 - x2

                                                     this example convergence is considerably slower. How large should n be to get better ac-

                                                           If we take n = 100, that is, use 100 rectangles, then the width of each rectangle is
                                                     ¢x = 11 - 02/100 = 0.01. Using the midpoint of each subinterval, we can easily gener-
                                                     ate the spreadsheet which we do not show here, because of its size (but is easily done on

                                                            The left and the right sums yield 3.120417 and 3.160417 as approximations to p,
                                                     still considerably inaccurate. We see that while there is some improvement as n, the num-
                                                     ber of rectangles, increases, in this particular example, n will need to be very large before
                                                     the approximation improves significantly. It will ultimately get better, but for a much
                                                     larger value of n. That is, the convergence is slow.

ter way of obtaining the areas with the calculator using Sigma notation.

Suppose you have a set of 30 data points, say 5x1, x2, x3, Á , x306 and you wanted to in-
dicate their sum, then you would write
                                                                                                                                           Sigma Notation
                                        x1 + x2 + x3 + Á + x30
        Mathematicians have developed a shorthand method for indicating such sums. We
write
                                                    30

                                                    a xk
                                                   k=1

     The Greek letter sigma 1©2 tells us to sum, the expression we are summing is xk,
we begin with the value of k = 1 and we stop with the value of k = 30. That is,

       Sigma notation is nothing more than a shorthand. We could proceed without it, but
it makes the writing of expressions involving sums much easier. We shall now use it to
help us represent the area of a region.
       We saw in the last section that while it is an easy matter to use larger and larger
spreadsheets to improve upon the approximation in computing the area of a region, we
would like to obtain the exact area. How might we go about doing that? The answer ap-
pears obvious: do exactly what we did on the examples in the previous section and let n,
the number of rectangles, become infinite. That is, we need to take a limit. This is where
the calculus comes into play. Before we do that, we first need to write the sums of the rec-
tangles slightly differently, using sigma notation.
       While we considered examples using the left, right or midpoint of each subinterval,
we saw that it really does not matter which point we used in each subinterval to construct
the top of the rectangles: we could use any point. Let us call c1 the x-value used in the first
subinterval, c2 the x-value in the second interval, and so on, giving cn the x-value in the                                                Riemann Sums
last (nth) interval. We let the width of each rectangle be ¢x. We shall assume that f is a
non-negative continuous function (we ll explain why later). The corresponding y-values
will be f1c12, f1c22, Á , f1cn2, and the area of the n rectangles are f1c12 ¢x,
f1c22 ¢x, Á , f1cn2 ¢x, respectively.
       Therefore, if we sum the areas of these n rectangles, we obtain an approximation
A n to the area of the region, namely,

       Let us define a more convenient notation to represent this limit. In motivating this
notation, we assume the function is non-negative, but it does not have to be. We draw an
infinitesimally thin representative rectangle.

       In essence, what we do is to find the sum of the area of an infinite number of such
thin rectangles, each of whose width is approaching zero. Suppose we call the width of
such a representative rectangle the differential dx and its height f(x). Then the (differen-                                               Definite Integral
tial) area of this representative rectangle is f(x)*dx (see Figure 1.)
       Now we sum the infinite number of the areas of such rectangles beginning at a and
ending at b. We use the integral symbol, which is an elongated S to indicate we are sum-
ming an infinite number of rectangles, and we indicate the a and b to show where we start

                                                            Thus, we see that if f is non-negative on [a, b] then f1x2 dx represents the area
                                                                                                                     3
                                                                                                                     a
                                                     of the region bounded by the curve and the x-axis over this interval. If the function is neg-
                                                     ative over some or all of the interval, then the symbol gives the sum of the signed areas of
                                                     the appropriate regions. In any event, the definite integral is a number which depends on
                                                     the sign of f, this number may or may not represent an area.
                                                            Basically, the notions of area and Riemann sums are nothing more than simple
                                                     geometry: adding up the areas of many rectangles. We move into the realm of calculus
                                                     when we consider the limit as n becomes infinite. Can we use the calculus to help us com-
      Fundamental                                    pute (1) in a simpler way? The answer to this question results in one of the most beautiful
       Theorem of                                    results in the calculus: the so-called Fundamental Theorem of Integral Calculus. Basi-
    Integral Calculus                                cally, this theorem says that if you can integrate f, then (1) is easily determined.

Let s go back and re-examine the idea presented in Figure 1. Basically, it tells us that
when we want to compute an area, we draw an incremental rectangle. The definite inte-
gral then gives the sum of the infinite number of these rectangles. We then use the Funda-
mental Theorem to compute the integral. We illustrate this remark in the next example.

This theorem states that for most functions, where the substitution method works on an in-
definite integral, it may be extended to the definite integral, provided we substitute for the
limits of integration as well. Moreover, once the complete substitution is made, we do not
have to return to the original variable of integration.

Sometimes, it is easier to integrate with respect to y to compute an area. That means in-
stead of summing vertical rectangles, we sum horizontal rectangles. This is useful in cases
when the equation of one or more of the curves is not a function of x, but can be written as
a function of y. For example, consider the equation y2 = x; this equation does not define
y as a function of x because to each x-value other than 0, we obtain two different y-values,
violating the definition of a function. However, if we think of x in terms of y, then this
does define a function of y. We illustrate the idea in the next example.

A and B.

       Recall, that when supply and demand equations are plotted on the same set of axes,
their intersection E1xe, pe2 is called the point of market equilibrium. It is characterized by
the fact that at the equilibrium price, supply and demand will be equal. If the price goes
above this value, the supply will increase and the demand decrease, causing an oversupply
and forcing the producers to lower their price. Similarly, if the price is below the equilib-
rium price, there will be a shortage followed by an upward adjustment in the market. Thus,
the equilibrium price is the price that the market determines for any given commodity.
       While pe is the market price for a given item, it often happens that the consumer is
willing to pay a higher price for the item, especially if it is an item that is greatly desired
by the consumer. Suppose only one item is available to the consumer, sold at the price
p(1); To sell two units of the item, the price would then be p(2); three units of the item
would have a price of p(3), and so on. However, the price paid by the consumer is actually
pe, so when one unit is sold, since the consumer is willing to pay the price p(1) (the value                                               Consumer and
the consumer attached to the item), the difference between the two prices 1p112 - pe2                                                     Producer Surplus
represents a surplus for the consumer. Similarly, for the second unit, a person would have
been willing to pay the price p(2) for that item (the value the consumer attaches to the
item), but actually pays pe, thus generating a (smaller) surplus. We can continue this
process until we reach equilibrium, see Figure 9, which shows the demand curve the item
and the price per item.

There are many different techniques of integration, but in an introductory text like this we
shall consider only one more method, which is one of the most powerful and is based only
on the product rule for derivatives; it is called integration by parts. We make the observa-
tion that if u and v are differentiable functions of x,                                                                                 Integration by Parts

                                       d           dv    du
                                          1uv2 = u    + v .
                                       dx          dx    dx
or multiplying by dx (writing in differential format)
                                         d1uv2 = u dv + v du
or rewriting
                                         u dv = d1uv2 - v du
We integrate each side of this equation, giving

                                            u dv = uv -           v du                                     (1)
                                        L                     L
(1) is called the integration by parts formula.
       Integration by parts does not appear to be a deep result, it is nothing more than the
reformulation of the product rule, yet we shall see that it is most effective in integrating
expressions which are the product of two different types of functions.
       In the event that we are evaluating a definite integral, the corresponding integration
by parts formula is

                                 row          Sign           Deriv.          Int.

       Basically, repeated integration by parts has the form

           +u1v2 - u2v3 + u3v4 + Á . + 1 -12nun - 1vn + 1-12n + 1                         unvn dx
                                                                                      L
       Note that the subscripts correspond to the row number in the table, and the signs
continue to alternate, the last term is the integral of the product of the last row with the ap-
propriate sign in the alternation process.
       In summary, we form three columns; a column of alternating signs (beginning with
+ ), a column of derivatives, beginning with u, and a column of the integrals, beginning
with dv (with all dx terms omitted). Whenever we stop, the integration by parts result is
obtained by multiplying the entries in the derivative column (along with the associated
sign) with the entry on the next row of the integral column (follow the slanted arrow),
when we get to the last row, we integrate the product (including the sign) of the derivative
and integral columns (following the horizontal arrow).
          We remark that integrals of the form      p1x2q1x2 dx, where p(x) is a polynomial
                                                 L
and q(x) is a function all of whose integrals are easily determined, can always be quickly
evaluated using tabular integration (integration by parts). Moreover, the objective is to
continue the process by adding rows until the last row has a zero in the derivative column
(as in Table 5).
       The table structure is just a short hand method of doing repeated integration by parts
a bookkeeping method and works well on most problems which require integration by
parts. It is especially convenient for other products of functions not considered in this text.

           6                       to Functions
                                   of Several Variables

                                                                      This chapter extends the notions of the previous chapters to functions of two
                                                                      or more variables. It also introduces the method of LaGrange multipliers,
                                                                      multiple integrals and their applications.

                                                     In Chapter 1, we introduced the notion of a function of two or more variables, we first re-
                                                     view what was done there and then continue with a visualization of such functions.
                                                            Productivity may depend on the amount of available capital as well and the number
      Function of                                    of units of labor available, that is, productivity is a function of the two variables, capital
    Several Variables                                and labor. The cost of an automobile may depend on the labor, cost of steel, fiberglass and
                                                     rubber, that is, the cost is a function of four variables. It follows that in realistic applica-
                                                     tions, we may often need to deal with functions of more than a single variable. The defini-
                                                     tion of function extends in a very natural way. Consider first the case of a function of two
                                                     variables. To each pair, (x, y), we associate a unique value z, written z = f1x, y2. The
                                                     definition extends is a natural way to any number of variables.
                                                            Computations with functions of two or more variables are handled the same way as
                                                     with a function of a single variable. You substitute for each variable as it appears in the
                                                     equation, as the next two examples illustrate.

                                                                                                                 4 81 = 3,
                                                                  3

                                                     and that 164 = A 2

                                                     The notions of limits and continuity may be extended to a function of several variables in
                                                     a very natural way. We shall not consider these generalizations here, as our objective is to
                                                     provide an elementary introduction to the subject. A more detailed treatment of these con-
                                                     cepts is left to a more advanced class. We remark that nice functions have limits and are
                                                     continuous. While we are not examining these concepts in details, we shall use them as
                                                     needed.
                                                           The idea of the difference quotient also can be generalized; shortly, we shall give
                                                     meaning to theses difference quotients.

                                                     dimensional surfaces, but will illustrate such surfaces as they prove useful to us. We
                                                     should, however, note that the three- dimensional- coordinate system takes the two-di-
                                                     mensional coordinate plane, and adds a third axis, the z-axis, to produce the three-dimen-
                                                     sional coordinate system. We draw the coordinate system in Figure 1. The positive x-axis
                                                     should be visualized as coming out of the page.

                                                                                                        z

                                                                         Figure 1: Three-Dimensional Coordinate System

                                                     The dotted portion of the axes represent the negative part of the axes. A two dimensional-
                                                     coordinate system divides the plane into four quadrants, a three-dimensional coordinate
                                                     system divides space into eight octants (to each of the four quadrants in the usual xy
                                                     plane, there are two choices for z, above or below the xy plane, giving the eight octants).
                                                            Note that the set of all points of the form (x, y, 0) is the x-y plane (the usual two-
                                                     dimensional plane), the set of all points of the form (x, 0, z) is the two-dimensional xz plane
                                                     and set of all points of the form (0, y, z) is the two-dimensional yz plane.
                                                            By plotting the points determined by the equation z = f1x, y2 on a three-
                                                     dimensional coordinate system, we obtain the graph of the surface. Surfaces may have ex-
        Surfaces

                                                     optimize a function, we will need to locate such points. A three-dimensional surface illus-
                                                     trates such points. For example, consider the surface in Figure 2.

       Our objective is now clear. Given a function of two variables, we need to determine                                                 Calculator Tips
how to locate its maximum and minimum values. What about a function of three or more

dimensional, so we clearly cannot draw its graph (it could, however, be visualized in three
dimensions for fixed values of one of its variables), we shall see that the methods consid-
ered will work higher dimensional problems as well.
