                                                             Each of these limits resemble the ordinary derivative, the first with respect to the
                                                     variable x, and the second with respect to the variable y, but there is a slight difference in
   Partial Derivative                                each difference quotient, namely, they involve a second variable. While there is a second
                                                     variable, notice that the second variable does not change in the quotient, for example
                                                                              f1x + h, y2 - f1x, y2
                                                     when computing lim                               , the variable y does not change, and when
                                                                          h:0             h
                                                                        f1x, y + k2 - f1x, y2
                                                     computing lim                              , the variable x does not change. Therefore, the
                                                                   k:0              k
                                                     first limit is nothing more than the ordinary derivative of f with respect to x, assuming y is
                                                     treated like it is a constant, and the second limit is the ordinary derivative of f with respect
                                                     to y, assuming x is treated like it is a constant. These limits are call partial derivatives.
                                                     More formally, we have the following definition:

                                                     DEFINITION 1 Given the function defined by the equation z = f1x, y2
                                                                                                               0z     0f
                                                     (a) the partial derivative with respect to x, denoted by      or    or zx1x, y2 or fx1x, y2 is
                                                                                                               0x 0x
                                                              f1x + h, y2 - f1x, y2
                                                          lim                           , assuming this limit exists.
                                                         h:0              h
                                                                                                               0z     0f
                                                     (b) the partial derivative with respect to y, denoted by     or     or zy1x, y2 or fy1x, y2 is
                                                                                                               0y 0y
                                                              f1x, y + k2 - f1x, y2
                                                          lim                           , assuming this limit exists.
                                                         k:0              k
                                                            You should note, that just like an ordinary derivative, a partial derivative has alter-
                                                     nate representations, that is, we may replace z with f in the various notations.
                                                            As a result of our previous observations, we can compute the partial derivative with-
                                                     out having to determine the limit (assuming they exist), namely by using ordinary differ-
                                                     entiation rules. Thus, to find the partial derivative with respect to x, we differentiate with
                                                     respect to x in the usual way, using the rules we have already developed, treating y as a
                                                     constant wherever it appears, and, similarly, to find the partial derivative with respect to
                                                     y, we differentiate with respect to y in the usual way, treating x as a constant wherever it
                                                     appears.
                                                                           0                                                 0
                                                            The notation     means to differentiate with respect to x, and     means to differenti-
                                                                          0x                                                0y
                                                     ate with respect to y, the symbol 0 resembles a partial d, to remind us that the differentia-
                                                     tion is partial, that is, we keep the other variables constant during the differentiation
                                                     process, it is sometimes called the partial or round d.

                                                     For functions of more than two variables, we can define the partial derivatives in the same
                                                     way as we did above; in terms of a limit of a difference quotient, keeping all variables
                                                     constant, except the one we are differentiating with respect to. We could then make the
                                                     same observation that this corresponds to the derivative with respect to the given variable,
                                                     keeping the other variables constant. We take this observation as the generalized definition
                                                     of a partial derivative.
                                                     DEFINITION 2 Given a function of two or more variables, to find the partial derivative
                                                     with respect to a given variable (assuming the partial derivative exists) use the ordinary
                                                     rules of differentiation with respect to this given variable, treating all other variables as if
                                                     they are constants.

Example 7
Find the points at which both partial derivatives are zero if
f1x, y2 = 2x3 - 6xy - 3y2 + 72y + 12.
Solution We are asked to find the simultaneous solution to fx1x, y2 = 0 and
fy1x, y2 = 0. We find that (verify!),

                                         fx1x, y2 = 6x2 - 6y
and
                                     fy1x, y2 = -6x - 6y + 72
Therefore, we must solve the system
                                            6x2 - 6y = 0
                                          -6x - 6y + 72 = 0
The first of these equations gives y = x2, substitution into the second equation gives
                                        -6x - 61x22 + 72 = 0
or
                                            x2 + x - 12 = 0
or
                                         1x + 421x - 32 = 0
yielding x = -4 or 3. Since y = x2, we have the corresponding y values of 16 and 9.
Thus, the two partial derivatives are zero at 1-4, 162 and (3, 9). The corresponding z-val-
ues are f1-4, 162 = 652 and f13, 92 = 309, and the points on the surface where both
partial derivatives are zero are 1- 4, 16, 6522 and(3, 9, 309).

The Cobb-Douglas production function is used by economists to relate productivity to
labor and capital. Let x represent the number of units of labor available, and y the number
of units of available capital. Then the number of units produced, z, is given by
                                                                                                                                           Cobb-Douglas
                                         z = f1x, y2 = Cxayb
                                                                                                                                        Production Function
where C 7 0 is a constant and the constants a and b are chosen to represent the charac-
teristics of the particular model. The partial derivative of the production function with re-
spect to x (labor) measures the rate of change of production with respect to labor when
capital is kept fixed. As in the case of a single variable, we may interpret this derivative as
a marginal function, that is, equal to the change in production when one additional unit of
labor is available (for constant capital), and is known as the marginal product of labor.
Similarly, the partial derivative of the production function with respect to y (capital) meas-
ures the rate of change of production with respect to capital when labor is kept fixed; this
partial derivative is equal to the change in production when one additional unit of capital
is available (for constant labor) and is known as the marginal product of capital.

In (a), the given production function, the statement
                                         f1gx, gy2 = gf1x, y2
is interpreted by economists as indicating they are constant returns to scale. That is, a pro-
portional increase in x and y results in the same increase in f. For example, tripling both
labor and capital results in a tripling of production.
       The result in (b) of the previous example is a special case of a theorem due to
Euler which we shall examine more fully in the exercises. In this particular example,
xfx1x, y2 + yfy1x, y2 = f1x, y2, which provides a simple economic interpretation. Re-
call that fx1x, y2 is the marginal product of labor and fy1x, y2 is the marginal product of
capital. It should make perfect sense that each factor, labor and capital, should be re-
warded at a level equal to its marginal product. (For example, if increasing labor by one
unit results in an increase of production of 100 units per month the meaning of marginal
product of labor then the new laborer should receive a monthly wage equivalent to the
100 units. Thus, the total reward to labor is xfx1x, y2. Similarly, yfx1x, y2 is the corre-
sponding reward to capital. The result xfx1x, y2 + yfy1x, y2 = f1x, y2 says that these
rewards total exactly to the amount produced.
       Level curves arise in a variety of applications. We consider another example from
economic theory. It is the Utility Function. Suppose we have two consumption items such
as x gallons of gasoline and y gallons of milk. x gallons of gasoline and y gallons of milk
together are called a bundle. We can assign a numerical value to each pair (x, y) thus creat-
ing a function of two variables. This function is known as the utility function and can be                                             Utility Functions and
thought of as the value the consumer places on the bundle. Thus u(x, y) is a function of                                               Indifference Curves
two variables and its value represents how much the consumer values x gallons of gaso-
line and y gallons of milk. Economic theory often uses the property that more is better .
In other words, if we compare two bundles, x1 gallons of gasoline and y1 gallons of milk
which have utility u1x1, y12, and x2 gallons of gasoline and y2 gallons of milk, which
have utility u1x2, y22, then the consumer will prefer the bundle with the greater value.
       A utility function is a function of two variables. That is, its graph is a three dimen-
sional surface, so we may consider their contours level curves. Since u is fixed on each
contour, that is, two points on the same contour have the same utility, the consumer is in-
different to the specific choice of x and y on a contour. Therefore, the contour is called an
indifference curve.

       It turns out that for smooth functions, these two mixed partial derivatives are always
the same as indicated in the following theorem.
THEOREM For the smooth function z = f1x, y2, we have fxy1x, y2 = fyx1x, y2
       The smoothness condition requires that the second partial derivatives all be continu-
ous in a given region. The proof of this theorem may be found in more advanced calculus
texts.

                                                         In this section we generalize the notions of extrema considered in Chapter 3 to functions
                                                         of two or more variables. The next definition deals with relative and (absolute) extrema.
                                                         DEFINITION 1 The function defined by the equation z = f1x, y2, is said to have
                                                         (a) a relative maximum at the point P(a, b, f(a, b)) if f1a, b2 Ú f1x, y2 for all points
                                                             (x, y) near the point P,
                                                         (b) a relative minimum at the point P(a, b, f(a, b)) if f1a, b2   f1x, y2 for all points
                                                             (x, y) near the point P,




       Applied Calculus for Business, Economics, and Finance, by Warren B. Gordon, Walter O. Wang, and April Allen Materowski. Published by Pearson Learning Solutions.
       Copyright © 2007 by Pearson Education, Inc.

(c) a maximum at the point P(a, b, f(a, b)) if f1a, b2 + f1x, y2 for all points (x, y) in the
    domain of f,
(d) a minimum at the point P(a, b, f(a, b)) if f1a, b2 * f1x, y2 for all points (x, y) in the
    domain of f,


Notice that at a relative maximum, the z-value is higher than all other nearby z-values, and
at a relative minimum, the z-value is smaller than all other nearby z-values. At a maxi-
mum, the z-value is higher than any other z-value on the surface, and at a minimum it is                                                        Extrema
smaller than any other z-value on the surface.
      Thus, for a function of two variables, we have the same distinction between relative
extrema and extrema as we have for a function of a single variable. The notion of relative
extrema and extrema generalize in a similar way to a function of any number of variables.
      How do we determine the relative extrema? Visualize a mountain and suppose you
are hiking to the peak, there are many different paths to the peak, but they all are going up
to the peak and descend after the peak. Clearly the peak is an example of a relative maxi-
mum. Consider Figure 1.



                                                     P




                         Figure 1: Illustrating a Relative Maximum



       If you think of each path through the mountain peak as a curve, then the tangent line
at the peak is horizontal to each of these curves. In particular, if we cut this smooth surface
at the peak with planes parallel to the xz and yz-planes, then the slopes of the tangent lines
we obtain are precisely the partial derivatives with respect to x and y, therefore, we have
that both fx and fy are zero at the relative maximum. Similarly, if we were descending a
valley (approaching a relative minimum point), the same would be true; see Figure 2.




                                                       P
                         Figure 2: Illustrating a Relative Minimum

                                                            We know that for a function of a single variable there were points where the deriva-
                                                     tive vanished which were not relative extrema, and, as a result, we defined the notion of
     Critical Points                                 critical points and then examined them to determine what they were. We now generalize
                                                     that definition.
                                                     DEFINITION 2 Any point in the domain of a function at which any first partial deriva-
                                                     tive does not exist or at which all first partial derivatives are simultaneously zero is called
                                                     a critical point.
                                                           This means, to find the critical point for a smooth function of two variables, we
                                                     solve the system of equations
                                                                                                    fx1x, y2 = 0
                                                                                                    fy1x, y2 = 0
                                                            For a smooth function of three variables, we solve
                                                                                                   fx1x, y, z2 = 0
                                                                                                   fy1x, y, z2 = 0
                                                                                                   fz1x, y, z2 = 0
                                                     and, similarly, for a function of any number of variables.
                                                           Recall that for a function of a single variable, we included in our definition of a crit-
                                                     ical point those points in the domain of the function at which the derivative failed to exist.
                                                     The same is true for a function of two or more variables; there are surfaces at which one
                                                     or more of the partial derivatives does not exist, yet the point may still be a relative ex-
                                                     tremum, consider Figure 3. The point P is a sharp point: neither partial derivative exists at
                                                     this point, yet the function has a relative maximum there. For the most part, we will deal
                                                     with smooth functions, so such critical points will not arise often.


                                                                                                           P




                                                           Figure 3: A Critical Point Where the Partial Derivatives Do Not Exist


                                                            It is possible for a function of two variables to have both partial derivatives be zero
                                                     at a point P and yet the point is neither a relative maximum or relative minimum. To visu-
                                                     alize this, we give a sketch of a surface that is called a saddle because it looks similar to a
                                                     saddle you would place on a horse.
                                                            Suppose you sat in the saddle. The point at which your bottom rests is a minimum
                                                     in one direction (from the front to the back of the saddle), but if you were mounting the
                                                     saddle, the point at which you were pulling your leg over (from side to side) is a maxi-
                                                     mum. Thus the point P in one direction is a maximum, in another a minimum. But for it to
                                                     be a relative maximum, it most be the highest point in all directions, and similarly, to be a
                                                     relative minimum, it must be the lowest point in all directions. See Figure 4.

If we could easily draw the sketch of a surface, then visually, we could determine if the
critical points are relative maxima or minima. It turns out, however, that there is a theorem
                                                                                                                                             Second Partial
for a function of two variables that is analogous to the second derivative test for a function
                                                                                                                                             Derivative Test
of a single variable; it is called the Second Partial Derivative Test. It gives us a simple
test by which we may classify the critical points. Before we state it, we define another
function used in this test, called the discriminant.
DEFINITION 3 For the smooth function z = f1x, y2 the discriminant, denoted by
D(x, y) is defined by

                          D1x, y2 = fxx1x, y2fyy1x, y2 - [fxy1x, y2]2
      You may note the absence of the mixed partial derivative fyx1x, y2, but remember
for smooth functions the two mixed partials are the same, so we could replace the squared
term by the product fxy1x, y2fyx1x, y2. It is simpler to write one of them squared.
THEOREM - SECOND PARTIAL DERIVATIVE TEST Suppose the smooth func-
tion defined by the equation z = f1x, y2 has a critical point when x = a and y = b, at
the point P(a, b, f(a, b)).

Case I: (a) If D1a, b2 7 0 and fxx1a, b2 7 0 then f has a relative minimum at P.
          (b) If D1a, b2 7 0 and fxx1a, b2 6 0 then f has a relative maximum at P.
Case II: If D1a, b2 6 0 then f has a saddle point at P.
Case III: If D1a, b2 = 0 then the test is inconclusive.
         While the proof of this theorem is beyond the scope of the text, some remarks are in
order.
(1) Note in Case I, fxx1a, b2 7 0 means that curves in the surface passing through the
    point P are concave upward, therefore, the critical point is a relative minimum. Simi-
    larly, if fxx1a, b2 6 0, the curves are concave downward, a relative maximum.
(2) While the conditions in Case I use fxx1a, b2 7 0, we could have just as well used
    fyy1a, b2 7 0 in its place. Since D1a, b2 7 0, that means the product
    fxx1a, b2fyy1a, b2 is positive and greater than [fxy1a, b2]2, implying that fxx1a, b2
    and fyy1a, b2 have the same sign.

                                                          1. Evaluate fx1x, y2, fy1x, y2, fxx1x, y2, fyy1x, y2 and fxy1x, y2
                                                          2. Find the critical points, that is, solve fx1x, y2 = 0 and fy1x, y2 = 0.

                                                             D = 0, test fails; if D 7 0 proceed to the next step.
                                                          4. Evaluate fxx at each critical point.
                                                          5. Classify each critical point.

While the second partial derivative test does generalize to functions of three or more vari-
ables, we will not do so here. Instead, we will be more concerned with computing their
critical points and, if needed, classify them other ways.
       Thus far, we have considered only relative extrema; what about the extrema them-
selves? We saw when we studied functions of a single variable that very often the relative
extrema turned out to be the extrema. It will happen that this often will be the case for
functions of two or more variables, that is, the extrema at interior points of the domain or
on the domain s boundary. When this happens, we will try to justify our conclusions by
means of a graph, by geometrical or physical considerations. Note, for example, the rela-
tive maximum in Figure 1 is in fact the maximum of the function, and the relative mini-
mum of the function in Figure 2 is its minimum. We also recall that if a function of a
single variable is continuous on a closed interval then it assumes both its maximum and
minimum values. This theorem generalizes to functions of two or more variables as well,
and we will leave its examination to the exercises.
       Consider the next example which illustrates the determination of the minimum of a
function. It illustrates the generalization of the optimization problems we considered in
Chapter 1. We shall show another method of solving such problems involving constraints
in the next section.

When physical or geometrical reasoning are not conclusive, we may try to use the defini-
tion of an extreme value. Suppose f has a relative minimum at (a, b) then any other point in
the domain may be written as 1a + h, b + k2. If we can show that
f1a + h, b + k2 - f1a, b2 Ú 0 for every choice of h and k, then f(a, b) is the minimum
of the function (Why?). Similarly for a maximum, where we have
f1a + h, b + k2 - f1a, b2          0. This approach may be difficult to apply when the func-
tion is complicated. Often, some algebraic manipulations are required with this approach,
see Exercise 23.

 6.4 The Method of Lagrange Multipliers
 »     Method of Lagrange

 »     Calculator Tips


In Chapter 3 we considered optimization problems subject to constraints. For example, in
finding the dimensions of the rectangle of largest area with a given perimeter. Such two
variable optimization problems were solved by using the constraint equation to solve for
one variable in terms of other and then reducing the problem to a single variable. In the
last section, we considered the problem of minimizing the surface area of a box if it was
required to have a given volume. This was a three dimensional minimization problem that                                                                         Method of Lagrange
was reduced to a two dimensional one by using the constraint to solve for one variable
in terms of the other two. The determination of the critical points of such optimization
problems can be found using a method developed by the mathematician Joseph Louis
Lagrange (1736 1813). While the proof of his theorem requires more advanced mathe-
matics, implementation requires nothing more than finding partial derivatives and solving
a system of equations.

532 * * * Section 6.4 The Method of Lagrange Multipliers

                                                      METHOD OF LAGRANGE Given the function defined by z = f1x, y2 subject to a
                                                      constraint c1x, y2 = 0, introduce a new variable l and define the function

                                                                                        L1x, y, l2 = f1x, y2 + lc1x, y2
                                                            Then the critical values of x and y of f subject to c = 0 will be among the critical val-
                                                      ues of L with respect to the three variables, x, y, and l.
                                                            Given the function defined by w = f1x, y, z2 subject to the constraint
                                                      c1x, y, z2 = 0, define the function
                                                                                   L1x, y, z, l2 = f1x, y, z2 + lc1x, y, z2
                                                             then the critical values of x, y and z of f will be among the critical values of L with
                                                      respect to the three variables, x, y, z, and l.
                                                             This method generalizes to any number of variables. We may also have additional
                                                      constraints as we shall see below. The symbol l is the Greek letter lambda and is called
                                                      the Lagrange multiplier.
                                                             While the method of Lagrange multipliers yields the critical points of f, it does not
                                                      identify which of those critical points are its maxima and minima. We will need to use
                                                      other methods, as indicated in the previous section to make this determination.
                                                             We note that some other texts write the equation of the form
                                                      L1x, y, z, l2 = f1x, y, z2 - lc1x, y, z2. The only difference in this form is the value for
                                                      l at the critical point of L. It will be the negative of the value we find. This does not effect
                                                      the critical points of f (our objective) in any way.

                                                      Example 1
                                                      Maximize f1x, y2 = xy subject to 2x + 2y = 10
                                                      Solution The constraint 2x + 2y = 10 needs to be written in the form

                                                                                        Ll1x, y, l2 = 2x + 2y - 10 = 0
                                                      (Note that Ll1x, y, l2 = 0 always yields the constraint equation. Why?)
                                                      We solve the system
                                                                                                    y + 2l = 0
                                                                                                    x + 2l = 0
                                                                                                 2x + 2y - 10 = 0
                                                      There are many ways to do the algebra; note that the first equation gives
                                                                                                       y = -2l
                                                      and the second gives
                                                                                                       x = -2l

       We could also find l, but we really do not need it, as we want the critical points of f.
Thus, f subject to the constraint c = 0 has as its only critical point (5/2, 5/2, 25/4). It s easy
to show, using the second partial derivative test, that this point is a relative maximum, and
if f has a maximum, it must be here.


Note that we could also have used x = -2l, y = -2l and substitute into the constraint
equation to find that l = -5/4, yielding x = y = 5/2.
       One way of solving the system of equations is to solve for all the variables in terms
of l, and then substitute for them in the equation Ll = 0 and solve for l. Alternately, as
we did above, we often may express the variables in terms of one variable and then substi-
tute into Ll = 0 to solve for this variable. We could always find l, but we really want the
critical points of f, not L.
       The best way of solving this last example and of solving most constrained optimiza-
tion problems in two variables, is by using the methods of Chapter 1, where we also have
an easy way of justifying the maximum. Note that the problem in Example 1 is asking you
to find the maximum area of the rectangle whose perimeter is 10.
       In the next example, we consider the method of Lagrange multipliers to solve the
minimization problem considered in the last section.

                                                          For a utility function, given a constraint on the items x, y, we may determine the
                                                     bundle that maximizes the utility function, as illustrated in the next example.

                                                     Example 5
                                                     Given the utility function u1x, y2 = xy2, suppose the price for each item x is $2 and for
                                                     each item y is $5 and the consumer has at most $60 to spend. What is his best buy?
                                                     Solution By best buy, we mean to maximize the utility function subject to the con-
                                                     straint 2x + 5y = 60. We may use Lagrange multipliers to solve this problem. We first
                                                     write the constraint in the form c1x, y2 = 2x + 5y - 60 = 0. Thus,

       We remark that just as a single definite integral may be represented as a Riemann
sum, a double integral may be also be represented as such a sum. In fact, suppose the re-
gion R is partitioned into n rectangles by drawing lines parallel to the coordinate axes that
cover the closed and bounded region R. Let the length of the longest diagonal of all these
rectangles is denoted by 7 ¢ 7, 1xi, yi,2 is any point in the ith rectangle, and ¢Ai the area of
this rectangle. Then it can be shown, for a continuous function f defined over R that
                                              n

                                                                                                                                                Volume
       You recall that with a single integral, area was nothing more then the limit of the in-
finite sum of infinitesimally small rectangles. In fact we considered a very thin representa-
tive rectangle of width dx and multiplied it by its height f(x) to obtain an element of area
                                                                                              b

f(x)dx, the infinite sum of all these rectangles became the area A =                              f1x2 dx. We may
                                                                                          3
                                                                                          a
use this sum analogy to realize that a volume is the infinite sum of infinitesimally thin rec-
tangular tubes, the area of each of the base tubes is dA and the height of each of these rep-
resentative tubes is z = f1x, y2. Their product f(x, y)dA is then the volume of this
representative tube. The infinite sum of the volume of all these tubes, which is the volume
of the solid is then the double integral V =                               f1x, y2 dA. We summarize with the
                                                                    LR L
following definition.


DEFINITION 1 Let R be a bounded closed region in the x-y plane, and let z = f1x, y2
be a non-negative continuous function. Then the volume of the solid bounded below by
the region R and above by the surface z = f1x, y2 is


                                                      V =          f1x, y2 dA
                                                            LR L

      The procedure for determining the volume of the solid, bounded above by the con-
tinuous function z = f1x, y2 and below in the x-y plane by the region R is as follows:
(1) Sketch the region R in the x-y plane, clearly indicating the curves bounding the region
    and its endpoint. Draw a representative rectangle to determine which are the bottom
    and top (or left and right) curves.
(2) Write the integral V =                   f1x, y2 dA as an iterated integral using the information
                                      LR L
        from (1).
(3) Evaluate the iterated integral
      We could generalize Definition 1 to determine the volume between two surfaces.
We do this in the exercises for the interested reader. Our objective in this section is to in-
troduce the concept of volume as an application of a double integral.

                                         and Linear Systems

                                                                      This Appendix introduces the elementary properties of matrices. It then
                                                                      examines the relationship between matrices and linear systems of equations.
                                                                      Matrices are an important tool in many different disciplines, therefore an un-
                                                                      derstanding of their properties is useful.

                                                     Matrices appear in a wide variety of applications. A matrix is used whenever there is a
                                                     need to store information. In most programming languages they are called arrays. In par-
                                                     ticular, they may be used to represent relations, collections of vertices and edges (called
                                                     graphs), or systems of equations. We begin by defining a matrix.
                                                     DEFINITION 1 A matrix is a rectangular array of numbers. We denote matrices by
                                                     upper case letters.
                                                            For example,
                                                                                                1             2          -1    0
                                                                                           A = +3             0           8    5*
                                                                                                2            -4           1    9
                                                     is a matrix with three rows and four columns. (The rows are horizontal while the columns
        Matrices                                     are vertical.) The dimension or size of this matrix is 3 * 4. Note that the dimension
                                                     is given in the form, row * column. The numbers in the matrix are called entries or
                                                     elements.
                                                           A matrix may have any number of rows and any number of columns. Some addi-
                                                     tional examples are:
                                                                             1        2       3        4          5
                                                                                                       1          1

                                                                                                   4        2
                                                                           0
                                                     B is a 4 * 5 matrix, C is a 1 * 4 matrix, D is a 3 * 1 matrix and E is a 2 * 2 matrix.
                                                     Any matrix consisting of one row is called a row vector. Thus, C is an example of a row
                                                     vector. The commas between the entries in C were put in for readability and could have
                                                     been omitted. Similarly, any matrix consisting of one column is called a column vector; D
                                                     is a column vector. The matrix E has the same number of rows and columns. Any matrix
                                                     with the same number of rows as columns is called a square matrix.
                                                            When identifying a particular entry in a matrix we always give its row location be-
                                                     fore its column location. Thus, the 2-3 entry of B is 11, the 3-2 entry of B is 34, the 1-2
                                                     entry of C is 2, the 3-1 entry of D is 0 and the 1-1 entry of E is 5.
                                                            In a square matrix, the main diagonal consists of those elements whose row and col-
                                                     umn positions are the same, that is, entries 1-1, 2-2, 3-3, etc. In other words, the main di-

In order to work with matrices, we need to define certain basic terms. We start with equal-
ity, addition, and scalar multiplication.
DEFINITION 2
 1. Two matrices are said to have the same size if and only if they have the same dimension.
 2. Two matrices of the same size are equal if and only if their corresponding entries are
    equal. That is, if A = 1a ij2m * n and B = 1bij2m * n then A = B if and only if a ij = bij
    for each pair (i,j).
 3. Two matrices of the same size may be added. Their sum is a matrix with the same di-
    mension. Each entry in the sum is obtained by adding the corresponding entries of the
    matrices summed. That is, if A = 1aij2m * n and B = 1bij2m * n, their sum A + B =
    C = 1cij2m * n, where cij = a ij + bij for each pair (i,j).

                                                          1kaij2m * n. The matrix 1-12A is denoted by the symbol - A.

                                                      To see that the definition of matrix addition is a natural one, consider the following. Sup-
                                                      pose the matrix A represents the profits, in thousands of dollars, (loss, if the entry is nega-
                                                      tive) that a company makes on the sale of each of 9 products during January, and B
                                                      represents its profits on the same items during February. Then the company s combined
                                                      profits for the two months are given by C. Thus, in the given matrices, the 1-1 entry indi-
                                                      cates a net loss of four thousand dollars for the product represented by that entry, and the
                                                      2-3 entry indicates a net profit of thirteen thousand dollars for that product.
                                                             Observe that for addition to be performed the matrices must be the same size. If two
                                                      matrices do not have the same dimension then addition is not defined. However, you
                                                      should convince yourself that when addition is defined, it satisfies the commutative and
                                                      associative laws. That is, A + B = B + A and A + 1B + C2 = 1A + B2 + C.

Again, if A represents the profits of a company, and we assume that the profits tripled,

      A zero matrix Z has the special property that if A is any matrix with the same di-
mension as Z, then A + Z = A. Given any matrix A, we have A - A = A + 1-A2 = Z.                                                              Zero Matrix
(This means that all the entries in Z are 0.) Note that there are an infinite number of zero
matrices, since to add Z to A means that A and Z have the same dimension. These observa-
tions mean that we can manipulate matrices like numbers in many algebraic operations.
For example, if
                                               A + B = C,
then adding -B to each side of the matrix equation yields
                           A + B - B = C - B, or A + Z = C - B,
or finally,
                                               A = C - B.

We are almost ready to define the product of two matrices. The definition will at first
seem unusual, but as various applications are discussed throughout the text, you will bet-
ter understand why the definition is chosen.
      Many students wonder why the product of two matrices is not simply defined to be
the matrix obtained by multiplying the corresponding entries of the two matrices in a
                                                                                                                                       Vector Multiplication
manner analogous to finding the sum of two matrices. In fact, there are mathematical sys-
tems in which such a definition is used but it has very limited application. To start with, it
would limit the definition to matrices of the same size. We shall see that the only restric-
tion imposed by our definition is that the number of columns of the matrix on the left
must equal the number of rows of the matrix on the right. This requirement leads directly
to the definition of vector multiplication which follows. Once vector multiplication is un-
derstood, the product of two matrices is easily obtained.
DEFINITION 1 - VECTOR MULTIPLICATION To multiply a row vector positioned
on the left with the same number of entries as a column vector on its right, the correspon-
ding entries are each multiplied together and the individual products are then summed.
      It is important to note that in accordance with Definition 1, the product of a row
vector with a column vector is a number.

Example 1
                                                           4
Compute the vector product of 11,             2,    32 # + 5 *.
                                                           6
Solution. The product is obtained by multiplying the corresponding entries and sum-
ming. Thus, the product is 112142 + 122152 + 132162 = 32.


It may first appear strange that the product of two vectors should be a number. However,
the following example may indicate why the definition is a natural one.

Example 2

at 32 cents per pound and 7 lb. of tomatoes at 78 cents per pound. Represent the
poundage order by a row vector, the prices as a column vector and use vector multiplica-
tion of the two vectors to determine the total cost.
Solution. Let r = 14, 5, 72 represent the poundage ordered of apples, potatoes and
tomatoes respectively, and the corresponding prices by the column vector

                                                      We are now ready to define multiplication of two matrices. We shall use, in our definition,
 Matrix Multiplication                                the vector multiplication of a row vector (on the left) by a column vector (on the right).
                                                      This will mean that we can only multiply matrices in which the number of columns in the
                                                      matrix on the left is the same as the number of rows in the matrix on the right. This will
                                                      also imply, as you shall see, that matrix multiplication is not commutative.
                                                      DEFINITION 3 - MATRIX MULTIPLICATION Let A = 1aij2M * K and B = 1bij2K * N.
                                                      Then the product

                                                                                                AB = C = 1cij2M * N

                                                      where cij = the vector product of the i-th row of A with the j-th column of B.
                                                            The definition indicates that the matrix on the left must have the same number of
                                                      columns as the matrix on the right has rows. The product matrix has the same number of
                                                      rows as the matrix on the left, and the same number of columns as the matrix on the right.
                                                      The ij entry of the vector product is the product of the i-th row of the matrix on the left
                                                      with the j-th column of the matrix on the right.

                                                      Example 3
                                                      Can a 2 * 5 matrix be multiplied on the right by a 5 * 7 matrix, and if it can, what is the
                                                      dimension of the product?
                                                      Solution. Since the number of columns in the matrix on the left (five) is the same as
                                                      the number of rows in the matrix on the right, the product is defined. It will have the same
                                                      number of rows as the matrix on the left (two), and the same number of columns as the
                                                      matrix on the right (seven). Thus the product is a 2 * 7 matrix.


                                                      Observe that the product of the matrices in the reverse order, the 5 * 7 matrix on the left
                                                      and the 2 * 5 matrix on the right, is not defined.

                                                      Recall that for any non-zero real number a, 1a = a1 = a. Given the matrix A M * N does
                                                      there exist a matrix which when multiplied by A leaves A unchanged? Rephrasing the
      Identity Matrix
                                                      question, is there a matrix that behaves like the number one? The answer is yes, but this
                                                      matrix is not always the same. If the matrix is on the right of A, then calling it IR * S, we
                                                      would have, A M * NIR * S = A M * N. In order for multiplication to be defined, we must
                                                      have R = N. (why?) Additionally, the number of columns in the product comes from the
                                                      number of columns in the matrix on the right, thus we have S = N. Therefore I is an
                                                      N * N (square) matrix. Similarly, if we multiply A on the left, now call the matrix IU * V,
                                                      and we have, IU * VA M * N = A M * N. As above, we find that U = V = M, and I is a
                                                      M * M square matrix. Since I is a square matrix, we write IN instead of IN * N, similarly
                                                      for IM. The matrix IN is called the identity matrix. For each value of N there is a different
                                                      identity. When there is no ambiguity, we shall omit the subscript N.
                                                            The question that still remains is what are the entries in I? It turns out that I has a
                                                      particularly simple form. All its diagonal entries are 1 and its non-diagonal entries are 0.
                                                      (The proof of this may be found in the exercises.) Thus,
                                                                                                                        1    0   0
                                                                                                    1     0
                                                                                             I2 = a         b,   I3 = + 0    1   0*.
                                                                                                    0     1
                                                                                                                        0    0   1
                                                      where I2 and I3 are the 2 * 2 and 3 * 3 identity matrices, respectively. It should be clear
                                                      what IN looks like for any N. It is an N * N matrix with ones along the main diagonal
                                                      and zeros elsewhere. You should try some simple examples to convince yourself that this
                                                      is correct.

      Inverse Matrix

                                                      a -1a = 1. Does there exist a matrix, which could be denoted by A-1, such that
                                                                                                        A-1A = AA-1 = I?

       When such a matrix exists, it is called the inverse. In order for both of these multi-
plications to be defined, A must be a square matrix (why?). However, even for a square
matrix, A-1 does not always exist. As you know, among the real numbers, only zero has
no reciprocal. However, there is an entire class of matrices that is analogous to the number
zero in this respect. Such matrices are called singular. A singular matrix is one that has no
inverse. If a matrix A has an inverse it is said to be invertible or non-singular. It may also
be shown that if A is a square matrix, and if AA-1 = I, then A-1A = I. That is, it is not
necessary to do both calculations in order to verify that A-1 is the inverse of A. Thus, if A
is a square matrix and A-1 is a left inverse, then it is also a right inverse! (See Exercise
33 for an example of a partial inverse.)
       For the moment we shall not be concerned about the process used to find an inverse.
Instead let us see how it may be used if it is known.

Table 1 is a summary of the various properties satisfied by matrices. We will leave their
verification to the exercises, but will assume familiarity with them. It is understood that all
multiplications and additions indicated in Table 1 are defined.

Table 1: Matrix Properties
                                   Properties of Matrices
   ADDITION
   A + B = B + A                              Commutativity
   A + 1B + C2 = 1A + B2 + C                  Associativity
   A + Z = A                                  Zero matrix exists
   MULTIPLICATION
   AB Z BA                                    Non-Commutativity
   1AB2C = A1BC2                              Associativity
   AI = A                                     Identity matrix exists
   A1B + C2 = AB + AC                         Distributivity over addition
   1B + C2D = BD + CD
   A1kB2 = kAB                                Associativity over scalar multiplication
   INVERSE AND IDENTITY
   AI = IA = A
   A-1A = AA-1 = I

                                                      As the preceding exercise clearly indicates, once the inverse of a coefficient matrix is
                                                      known, the system of equations is easily solved by matrix multiplication. However, we
                                                      must ask ourselves if this is an efficient method. After all, we have yet to determine the
                                                      amount of labor involved in finding the inverse matrix. Clearly, once the inverse is calcu-
                                                      lated, the remaining labor is minimal.
                                                             We know that not every linear system of equations has a unique solution. For exam-
                                                      ple, consider the equations
                                                                                                     2x + y = 6
                                                                                                     4x + 2y = 9
                                                      As you know, the graphs of these two equations are parallel lines, which never intersect.
                                                      Hence, the lines have no points in common and this system has no solution. Therefore, the
                                                      coefficient matrix corresponding to this system cannot have an inverse and must be a sin-
                                                      gular matrix. It is clear that there is relationship between the existence of a unique solu-
                                                      tion to a linear system of equations and the existence of the inverse of its coefficient
                                                      matrix. It is this relationship that motivates the examination of linear systems in the next
                                                      section. In fact, after examining a procedure for determining the solution to a linear sys-
                                                      tem of equations, we shall discover a procedure for finding the inverse of a matrix, when
                                                      it exists.

                                                        In the previous section we indicated that there is a connection between solutions of sys-
                                                        tems of linear equations and the existence of the inverse of a matrix. It will prove useful to
                                                        examine systems of linear equations in some detail before we return to the question of
                                                        finding the inverse of a matrix, when it exists.
                                                               When a system has two unknowns, we usually call them x and y, when there are
                                                        three, we may denote them x, y and z. However, when there are more than three, say n un-
                                                        knowns, it is convenient to use subscripts and name them x1, x2, x3, x4, Á , xn. Thus, a
                                                        system of m linear equations in n unknowns may be written as

                                                                                    a 11x1 + a12x2 + a 13x3 + Á + a1nx1n = b1
                                                                                    a21x1 + a22x2 + a 23x3 + Á + a2nx2n = b2
                                                                                                                                                                (1)
                                                                                                           o
                                                                                   am1x1 + a m2x2 + a m3x3 + Á + amnxmn = bm

                                                        Rather than work directly on this set of m equations in n unknowns, we store all the im-
                                                        portant information in a matrix, called the augmented matrix, which is formed by entering
    Augmented Matrix

                                                        hand side of the system. Although is not necessary, we indicate the separation between the
                                                        coefficient matrix and the right hand side by a vertical line. Thus, the augmented matrix
                                                        corresponding to (1) is

                                                                                          a 11   a 12     a 13     Á      a 1n     b1
                                                                                          a 21   a 22     a 23     Á      a 2n
                                                                                      §                                          4 b2 ¥                         (2)
                                                                                                            o                       o
                                                                                          am1    am2      a m3     Á      amn      bm

                                                        thought of as being there. Thus, if a system of equations is written in the matrix form
                                                        AX = B, then the augmented matrix has the form 1A B2

Given a linear system of equations, our objective is to determine its solution. If a solu-
tion exists, the system is said to be consistent, It may happen that the system has no so-
lution, in which case we say that the system is inconsistent. In this section we shall only
consider systems possessing unique solutions. Other cases will be examined in the next
section.
      There are several ways to solve systems of equations but all come down to the
same thing; that is, to perform operations on the given system that will replace it by an
equivalent system (one with the same solution set), from which we may more easily de-
termine the solution. We shall see that it is more convenient to perform the calculations
on the augmented matrix rather then on the system itself. Thus, we have to understand
exactly what types of operations are permitted on the augmented matrix. Since the aug-
mented matrix is shorthand for the system, any operation that may be performed on the
system may be performed on the matrix. In particular, there are three operations that are
allowed when working with a system of equations: (1) Swapping (Interchanging) any
two equations, (2) Multiplication of every term on both sides of an equation by a non-
zero constant, (3) Adding a multiple of one equation to any other equation. (To be pre-
cise, operation (3) means that we can replace any equation by a new equation obtained
by adding to the original equation any multiple of another equation in the system. It is
important to keep in mind that the number of equations in the system should remain the
same.)

Example 3
Solve the following system of equations.
                                                 x + 4y = -2
                                                 2x - 3y = 7




Applied Calculus for Business, Economics, and Finance, by Warren B. Gordon, Walter O. Wang, and April Allen Materowski. Published by Pearson Learning Solutions.
Copyright © 2007 by Pearson Education, Inc.
580         Appendix A.3       Gauss-Jordan Reduction

                                                      Solution. Using what is usually referred to in preliminary algebra courses as the addi-
                                                      tion method, we try to eliminate one of the unknowns from one of the equations. One
                                                      way to do this is to multiply the first equation by -2 and add it to the second equation,
                                                      thus eliminating x from the second equation. Actually, we replace the second equation by
                                                      the new one. Denoting the two equations as e1 and e2, we can indicate this step by writing
                                                      e2 = -2e1 + e2. (e2 represents the modified second equation.) Thus, our system of equa-
                                                      tions is now

                                                                                                    x + 4y = - 2
                                                                                                       - 11y = 11
                                                      We now see that we can divide the second equation by -11 and solve for y.
                                                                                                     x + 4y = - 2
                                                                                                      + y = -1
                                                      We could substitute y = - 1 in the first equation and solve for x. Instead, let us continue
                                                      to use the addition method to eliminate y from the first equation. In other words add
                                                      -4 times the second equation to the first. In symbols, the modified equation
                                                      e1 = e1 + 1-42e2. This leaves
                                                                                                            x = 2
                                                                                                            y = -1
                                                      There is no equivalent system for which it could be any easier to read off the solutions!


                                                      You should realize that the unknowns x and y played no role in the method of solution. All
                                                      of the operations performed on the system effected only the coefficients and the right
                                                      hand side constants. In other words, the allowable operations could just as easily have
                                                      been performed on the entries in the augmented matrix used to represent this system of
                                                      equations. Thus we have the following definition.
                                                      DEFINITION 1 - ELEMENTARY ROW OPERATIONS The following operations
                                                      are called elementary row operations:

                                                      (1) Swapping any two rows of the augmented matrix,
                                                      (2) Multiplying every entry in a row by a non-zero constant,
                                                      (3) Adding a multiple of one row to the corresponding entries of any other row.

                                                            Performing these operations on the augmented matrix produces a new matrix. The
                                                      solution set of the system represented by this modified matrix is identical to the original
                                                      solution set.
                                                            The question that naturally arises is what is our objective? If we are to perform ele-
                                                      mentary operations to the augmented matrix, to what do we want to transform it? There
Gauss Jordan Reduction
                                                      are several possibilities. Our objective is to reduce it to a form that is so simple that we are
                                                      able to read off the unique solution directly from the matrix just as we did for the two by
                                                      two system in Example 3. Now, take a look back at that solution. In matrix form, the
                                                      augmented matrix was
                                                                                                        1   0    2
                                                                                                    a         `    b
                                                                                                        0   1   -1

                                                      hand side gives the solution. Thus, in general, our goal shall be to transform the left hand
                                                      side of the augmented matrix to the Identity matrix. Once we do this, the solution will be

on the right. This kind of reduction is called Gauss Jordan Reduction. In short, we begin
with the augmented matrix, and use elementary operations on it so that A is transformed
into I. Pictorially, we represent the procedure as

                                        1 A B2 : 1 I C2
C is the resulting right hand side after the operations have been performed. There are many
ways to achieve the desired reduction, the algorithm that we choose is the following:

                         Gauss-Jordan Reduction Algorithm
    1. Construct the augmented matrix from the given system of equations.
    2. Choose any diagonal entry from the coefficient matrix portion of the aug-
       mented matrix not yet selected and convert it to 1. This 1 is called a leading
       one or pivot.
    3. Use the pivot (leading one) from the preceding step to eliminate all non-zero
       entries in its column, called the pivotal column. If the left hand side of the
       modified augmented matrix is the Identity matrix the reduction is complete,
       otherwise go to Step 2.

It is necessary to explain two terms used in the above algorithm; convert and eliminate. To
perform either of these actions, we may use the elementary operations described above.
(1) To convert any non-zero entry to a 1, we may multiply every entry in its row by the
    reciprocal of the selected entry.
(2) The elimination of the non-zero entries in the pivotal column may be accomplished
    by multiplying the row containing the pivot (leading one) by the negative of the entry
    we wish to eliminate, and then add this modified row to the row containing that entry.
We illustrate the algorithm by the next few examples.

Observe that the coefficient matrices for the two systems are identical. The augmented
matrix needed to find x and z is
                                                       3       5 1
                                                   a            ` b

and the augmented matrix needed to find y and w is
                                                       3       5 0
                                                   a            ` b
                                                       2       3 1
Of course, we could perform separate row reductions on each of these augmented ma-
trices, but it is immediately apparent that to reduce the left hand side of each of the aug-
mented matrices to the identity would require exactly the same operations. Instead, we
form another matrix, the left hand side of which is the above coefficient matrix, but with
two columns, each column representing the right hand side of one of the above systems.
Thus, we have the following matrix,
                                                  3        5 1             0
                                              a             `                b
                                                  2        3 0             1
Observe that the right hand side of this matrix is precisely the Identity matrix. This is no
coincidence. It occurred because the product of A and its inverse yield I.
      We now perform row operations on this matrix, so that the left hand side becomes
the Identity. When this happens, the first column on the right (column 3) gives the solu-
tion for x and z, and the second column on the right (column 4) gives the solution for y
and w. Thus, the right hand side of this matrix becomes the inverse. We shall actually per-
form the reductions in Example 8. First, we generalize the above discussion.
      Given the square matrix A, to find its inverse form the matrix

right hand side will then be the inverse matrix. Pictorially, the algorithm is

We know that not every matrix is invertible. Suppose we are given a singular matrix and
we apply this algorithm. We will be unable to get the identity on the left hand side. What
will appear instead will be a row containing zeros. Thus, from this algorithm, it will also
be obvious (at some point in the reduction process) if a matrix is singular.

Our next example illustrates what happens when one tries to find the inverse of a singular
matrix by using Gauss Jordan Reduction. As you will see a row of zeros appears on the
left hand side, making it impossible to select a pivot element with which to continue the
process. Thus, given any matrix, if it is invertible the reductions illustrated above result in
the Identity appearing on the left and the inverse on the right. If it is not invertible, a row
of zeros will appear at some stage bringing the reduction process to a halt.

                                                      Gauss Jordan Reduction performs three operations on a matrix, swaps two rows, multi-
                                                      plies any row by a non-zero constant, and adds a multiple of one row to a multiple of an-
      Calculator Tips
                                                      other row. These three operations can be done by the calculator. In performing these
                                                      reductions on a matrix, it will be necessary to rename and store the modified matrix after
                                                      each operation is performed. We shall illustrate, but first indicate the three corresponding
                                                      commands, with their syntax that is to be used to perform these reductions.
                                                             Suppose we have stored the matrix named a in the calculator s memory. The com-
                                                      mand (found in the Catalog, or may be entered by hand)
                                                                                                         RowSwap1a, m, n2 : a1
                                                      interchanges row m and row n and stores this new matrix as a1.
                                                                                                             mRow1m, a, r2 : a2
                                                      multiplies row r of matrix a by the constant m and stores this new matrix, renamed as a2.
                                                                                                      mRowAdd1m, a, I, J2 : a3
                                                      multiplies row I by the constant m, adds the modified row to row J, and stores this new
                                                      matrix as a3.
                                                             Essentially, these three commands automate the reduction process, doing all the al-
                                                      gebraic manipulations for us. (We shall see in the next section, that we can further auto-
                                                      mate this process to a single calculator command.) Our present goal is to emphasize an
                                                      understanding of the reduction process without getting bogged down with the intermedi-
                                                      ate arithmetic calculations. Note that after you have finished the reduction you will need
                                                      to clear the stored matrices from memory. If you have used two or more characters to
                                                      name the matrix using Clear from a-z option,( F6) will not work. Instead, you will need to
                                                      use the Var-Link key, located above the key, to delete these stored matrices from mem-
                                                      ory. Scroll down to each named matrix, press F1 and choose the delete option. You ll need
                                                      to confirm the deletion by pressing Enter twice.
                                                             We illustrate the three commands by reducing the augmented matrix of the system
                                                      given in Example 7.

 A.4 Inconsistent Linear Systems and Systems
                with Infinitely Many Solutions

In the previous section, we considered only systems with as many equations as unknowns.                                                          Alternative Theorem
That is, systems for which the coefficient matrix is square. In that case, we saw that the sys-
tem has a unique solution if and only if the coefficient matrix is non-singular. That leaves
two questions. First, what about systems for which the coefficient matrix is singular? Sec-
ond, what about systems in which the number of equations and unknowns are not the same?
The following theorem, called the Alternative Theorem, indicates all the possibilities.


     Alternative Theorem
     Given any system of linear equations, there are three alternatives:
     (1) the system has a unique solution,
     (2) the system has no solution,
     (3) the system has an infinite number of solutions.


PROOF Either the system has a unique solution or it does not. If the system does not
have a unique solution there are again two possibilities: Either there is no solution, or
there is more than one solution. To complete the proof we must show that the alternative
that there is more than one solution implies that there are an infinite number of solutions.
We write the system in the matrix form AX = B. Let X1 and X2 be two solutions to the
system. That means that each satisfies the equation AX = B. Thus, we have

                                             AX1 = B and AX2 = B
Observe that X1 - X2 satisfies the equation AX = Z, where Z is the zero column vector.
To see this, consider
                            A1X1 - X22 = A1X12 - A1X22 = B - B = Z.
