                                                      Let k be any real number and let W = k1X1 - X22 + X1 (note that there are an infinite
                                                      number of choices for W, each k produces another W). Consider
                                                                        AW = A1k1X1 - X22 + X12 = A1k1X1 - X222 + A1X12
                                                                           = kA1X1 - X22 + A1X12 = kZ + B = B.
                                                      For any k, W is a solution to the system. Thus, we have shown that if a linear system has
                                                      more than one solution, it has an infinite number of solutions.
                                                      *
                                                      We remarked in the last section that if a system has no solution it is said to be inconsis-
                                                      tent, and a consistent system is one which has a solution, which means either a unique so-
  Inconsistent Systems
                                                      lution or an infinite number of solutions. The immediate question is what makes a system
                                                      inconsistent? Think of each equation in a system as a piece of information, a clue to the
                                                      identities of the unknowns. Now we may answer that the system will be inconsistent when
                                                      the clues are contradictory. For example, consider the system
                                                                                                       x + y = 7
                                                                                                       x + y = 9
                                                      Clearly, x + y cannot be equal to both 7 and 9 at the same time! Thus, this system is in-
                                                      consistent, the information (the two equations) is contradictory. Geometrically, the equa-
                                                      tions represent two parallel lines. As parallel lines do not intersect, the system has no
                                                      solution. Certainly, the case of an inconsistent system with two unknowns requires no de-
                                                      tailed examination. However, we are interested in recognizing when any linear system is
                                                      inconsistent, so we shall take the above example a little further. Let us write the above
                                                      system as an augmented matrix and perform the usual reductions on its rows.

                                                                                a   ~
                                                                                    1 1 7
                                                                                       ` b r2 = - r1 + r2 : a
                                                                                                              1                  1   7
                                                                                                                                   ` b
                                                                                    1   1     9                             0    0   2
                                                      The last row means that 0x + 0y = 2, or 0 = 2. This is an absurdity, and we must con-
                                                      clude that the system is inconsistent. In general, given any linear system, proceed in the
                                                      usual manner. If at any time you arrive at a row which has all zeros on the left and a
                                                      non-zero number on the right, it means that the system is inconsistent, that is, it has no
                                                      solution.

                                                                                                  4x + 9y + 10z = 7

The next case to consider is how to determine when a linear system has an infinite number
of solutions, and in this case, how to describe the solutions. It turns out that this is a fairly
                                                                                                                                           Infinitely Many
straight-forward problem. This case is not new to you, it was studied in algebra. Consider
                                                                                                                                              Solutions
the system of equations
                                                x + 2y = 3
                                                x + 2y = 3
where we have the same equation written twice. There is a simple point to be underscored
with this example. If we again think of each equation as a piece of information, then the
above example indicates that the two pieces of information are not independent, in fact we
really have only one piece of information. One of the equations is redundant. This is typi-
cal of systems of equations with infinitely many solutions. The system reduces to one in
which the equations are consistent and the number of unknowns exceeds the number of
equations. Here we are asked to solve a system containing the single equation
x + 2y = 3. Geometrically, this single equation represents a line. We know that a line
contains an infinite number of points and the coordinates of any point on the line satisfy
the equation and give a solution. It is a simple matter to describe all the solutions. We
solve the equation for x, obtaining
                                               x = 3 - 2y
Now we are free to choose any number for y and substitute it into the above equation to
find the corresponding x-value. (Of course, we could also have chosen to solve for y in
terms of x.) We may think of y as being a free variable, sometimes called a parameter.
Now x is thought of as being determined by y. To emphasize this interpretation, we write
the solution as
                                                    y = k
and
                                               x = 3 - 2k.
Sometimes, it is convenient to write the answer as an ordered pair in the form 13 - 2k, k).
Where of course, the first member of the ordered pair is x and the second is y.
     If we solve the above problem with the two equations, using the augmented matrix,
we have,

                          a   ~
                              1 2 3
                                 ` b r2 = -r1 + r2 : a
                                                       1                   2   3
                                                                             ` b
                              1   2     3                             0    0   0
Unlike the inconsistent case, systems with an infinite number of solutions may often have
entire rows (both the left and right hand side) with only zero entries. (If you wish, you
may omit these rows as they occur, or keep them together as the bottom rows of the ma-
trix.) Notice that the x variable is represented by a leading one in the diagonal position of
this last matrix (the 1-1 entry), but it is impossible to obtain a 1 for the variable y, which
becomes the free variable.
       Summarizing, our object is to perform Gauss Jordan Reduction on the augmented
matrix, obtaining leading ones in the diagonal positions on the left hand side of the

The original augmented matrix has 4 rows. We now have two non-zero rows in the last
matrix. Therefore, there can only be two 1 s in the diagonal positions on the left. Thus, we
have completed the row reductions. We have,
                                         x + 4z - 2w = 16
                                         y - 3z + 7w = -14
Solving for x and y in terms of the free variables z and w we have,
                                         x = 16 - 4z + 2w
                                         y = -14 + 3z - 7w
As before, we let z = k and w = l, we have
                                         x = 16 - 4k + 2l
                                         y = -14 + 3k - 7l
                                         z =   k
                                         w =   l
The solution to this system involves the two free variables, k and l. For each choice of k
and l, we obtain another solution. Sometimes we describe this by saying the system has a
two parameter family of solutions.


Suppose we have a system in which the number of unknowns is greater than the number
of equations. The coefficient matrix will not be square and our algorithm instructs us to
use elements along the diagonal of the coefficient matrix as the pivots. So, what do we
do? Consider the following example.

Example 4
Solve the system of equations
                                        x - y + z + w = 6
                                       2x - 3y + 3z + w = 7
                                        x + y - z - 3w = 4

Solution. We have four unknowns and three equations. We may mentally add a row of
all zeroes to the bottom of the matrix, giving us four equations and a square coefficient

                                                      However, it is really not necessary to insert the row of zeroes. In essence, our last pivot is
                                                      simply not a diagonal entry on the left hand side. The first two pivots(leading ones) were
                                                      the 1-1 and 2-2 entries, but now the only non-zero entry in the last row is the 3-4 entry,
                                                      which we select as our pivot (leading one). Continuing with this pivot with the zero row
                                                      removed, we have

                                                      tain the leading ones (pivots)and zeros may be generalized as follows: define the leading




      Applied Calculus for Business, Economics, and Finance, by Warren B. Gordon, Walter O. Wang, and April Allen Materowski. Published by Pearson Learning Solutions.

                                                        Appendix A.4      Inconsistent Linear Systems and Systems with Infinitely Many Solutions                   599

one (pivot) to be the first non-zero entry of a row (assuming the row s entries are not all
zero); all rows consisting entirely of zeros shall be placed together at the bottom of the ma-
trix. In any two rows, not all zero, the leading one of the lower row will always be to the
right of the leading one of the upper row. Any matrix having this property is said to be in
row echelon form. In addition, if all the other entries in the column containing the leading
one are zero, then the matrix is said to be in reduced row echelon form, or rref for short.                                                               rref
       This generalization enables us to solve problems like the last example without the
insertion (or consideration) of imaginary rows containing all zero entries. The objective is
now to put the matrix in rref.
       What about a system in which the number of equations exceeds the number of un-
knowns? Let us look at such a case.

Example 5
Find two numbers such that the first is six more than twice the second, the second is three
more than the first, and five times the second plus 21 is equal to twice the first.
Solution. Let the first number be x and the second be y. Now, the first is six more than
twice the second, means that x = 2y + 6.
        The second is three more than the first, means that y = x + 3.
        Five times the second plus 21 is equal to twice the first, means that 5y + 21 = 2x.
       We now have three equations and two unknowns. In order to use our standard
method to solve the system, we first rewrite them in the usual order. That is, each must be
in the form ax + by = c. Thus,
                                               x - 2y = 6
                                              -x + y = 3
                                              2x - 5y = 21
We now set up our augmented matrix, but how do we choose a pivot? We use the diagonal
of the first two equations to determine the pivots. However, as we do our row reductions,
we shall work on all the rows.

The last row is all zeroes and we can read the solution from the first two rows: x = -12
and y = -9. You should convince yourself that had the last number in the third equation
been anything other than 21, the last row would reduce to zeroes on the left hand side but
not a zero on the right. Hence, the system would have been inconsistent.


In summary, given any system of equations, we know that there are three alternatives re-
garding its solution: there is a unique solution, no solution, or an infinite number of solu-
                                                                                                                                                   Calculator Tips
tions. It may not be obvious by inspection, which is the case, but performing
Gauss-Jordan Reduction on the augmented matrix (that is, obtain the rref of the aug-
mented matrix) will soon determine the proper alternative.
      Now that we know that Gauss-Jordan Reduction is nothing more than finding the reduced
row echelon form of a matrix, we can use a command from the calculator that will automatically
